asi.next: apply .auto/exp26/split_lg4.py then .auto/lane_prof.sh on board 3 to split prepare vs gather per call; if the gather owns the 3.4 ms, test a serial (unsplit) small-n gather, which is bit-exact by construction

description:
Experiment 27 - two screens whose absence had already cost board time, both run in one kbench image on board 3, and both come back saying "nothing here" with numbers: MEASURED, no shipping change (decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward; only a NEEDLE_KBENCH image ran, which by design never executes the request path - labelled, not a speed result).

SCREEN 1, WAKE LATENCY, retires a candidate before it costs a board. `rows_dual_core()`'s comment in main.c has always said "~15 us handshake", and that number is what has kept small-split ideas off the table while also keeping them alive: `nd_cq_prepare` hands the splitter only ngroup = 8 groups of a 128-point FWHT, run #343 measured one prepare at 0.156 ms, and there are ~12-20 prepares per token, so if waking a *parked* worker cost a tick (this is a 100 Hz-tick build, 2.4 M cycles) then tens of small splits per token would be worth percent-scale. Measured directly, min of 15 rounds, trivial pure function, worker parked via vTaskDelay(3 ms) before the timed split: serial = 10 cycles, split (hot) = 33, split (parked) = 33, so **the wake is 23 cycles = 0.10 us and is identical hot and parked**, for units = 2, 4, 8, 16 and 64 alike. The ledger's 15 us was the cost of the work in the job it was measured on, not of the handshake. Consequence, stated so it cannot come back: the upper bound on "run small jobs serially" is 23 cycles x ~30 small splits = 690 cycles = 0.003 ms/token = **+0.001 %**, and the reverse play (lowering the threshold to split nrows = 2-3, which is the sampler gather at n <= 3) is bounded by +0.03 %. Neither is buildable against a 0.2 % bar, and the shipping `half < 2` is already generous. The candidate applicator is kept at .auto/exp27/apply_serial_threshold.py with that arithmetic in its docstring, and was deliberately never flashed.

SCREEN 2, the banked multi-row differential, delivered and PASSING. Run #333's first integrated build of the 4-bit row walker diverged (device_output_exact 5/17, token_delta 175) while measuring *faster*, because `nd_gemv4_rows_tie1()`'s row epilogue re-stepped `packed`/`norms` that its word loop had already advanced a whole row, and the isolation screen called the kernel once per row where the *caller* does that stepping - so no single-row test could see it. `bench_rowrange()` now compares the range form against R single-row calls, row for row, on real archive bytes, both built through the same nd_gemv4_ctx layout the shipping dispatcher uses: **mismatch = 0 of 24 rows at chunk = 1, 12 and 24** (one row, a half split, a whole one-core sweep). By-product worth recording: `find_row4_tensor` resolves to the 4-bit *embedding* (out 8192, in_pad 768, ngroup 6, rowbytes 384), so the shipped 4-bit kernel is eligible for the sampler gather too - worth ~0.01 % at mean_n 6.7, which is why it stays unshipped.

FLOOR RE-CHECK done on the same image's own numbers, closing the last two unpriced per-call costs: `nd_cq_lut_build` = 32,598 cycles = **13.6 us per call** (0.014 ms, an order below the 0.135 ms this ledger has been quoting) for 8 multiplies + 16 adds + 16 contiguous 64 B-line stores per pair, already split by pair range, i.e. ~2.1 cycles/op; and `nd_cq_prepare`'s 0.156 ms = 37.4k cycles against ~20k ops of copy + memset + FWHT(6 groups x 7 stages x 64 butterflies) + scale pass = ~2 cycles per op, with FWHT unroll already a measured null. Both are at the scalar floor, so `prep+lut` (3.6 ms/token of a 197 ms token) contains nothing collectable.

TOGETHER WITH RUN #343 THIS MAKES THE TOKEN FULLY ATTRIBUTED: every phase has a measured mechanism behind it, and the ~1 % bench-to-request residue reconciles against per-call numbers (projection 0.23 ms + emit 0.10 ms + piece/argmax ~0.7 ms + longer context) instead of the retired 3.8/5.7 ms projection figures, which were timer-normalisation artefacts. Asset kept in the tree: bench_wake() + bench_rowrange() in esp32/main/kbench.c (kbench-gated, so a shipping configure never evaluates the branch; also saved as .auto/exp27/kbench-exp27.patch after an uncommitted-bench loss taught the rule that research code gets a patch file before any bulk `git checkout`).

asi.hypothesis: Two screens whose absence cost real board time: (1) what does a cross-core split actually cost when the worker is PARKED - rows_dual_core's comment says ~15 us and nd_cq_prepare splits only 8 FWHT groups, so if a parked wake were a tick, ~30 small splits per token would be worth a percent; (2) the multi-row differential for nd_gemv4_rows_tie1 whose absence cost run #333 its first build.
asi.measured_wake: KB WAKE: serial=10, split_hot=33, split_parked=33, wake=23 cycles for units=2,4,8,16,64. The handshake is 23 cycles (0.10 us), identical hot and parked, so the ledger's ~15 us comment is off by ~65x and is the hot-loop cost of the WORK, not the wake.
asi.candidate_retired_off_device: serial-for-small-jobs (ND_SPLIT_SERIAL_HALF): upper bound 23 cycles x ~30 small splits = 690 cycles = 0.003 ms/token = +0.001 %. Never build it. The shipping half<2 threshold is already generous, and LOWERING it (splitting nrows=2-3) is bounded by the sampler gather at n<=3, i.e. +0.03 %, also below bar. Patch kept as .auto/exp27/apply_serial_threshold.py with this arithmetic in its docstring so the idea cannot come back.
asi.measured_rowrange: KB ROWRANGE out=8192 in_pad=768 ngroup=6 rowbytes=384 chunk=1/12/24 mismatch=0/24 in every chunk size: the row-range kernel equals R single-row calls on real archive bytes. The banked test now exists and passes; note find_row4_tensor found the 4-bit EMBEDDING (out=8192, rowbytes=384 = 768 4-bit weights), so the shipping 4-bit kernel is also eligible for the sampler gather - still worth only ~0.01 % at mean_n 6.7.
asi.floor_recheck: lut build = 32,598 cycles = 13.6 us per call (0.014 ms, not 0.136 ms) at 2.1 cycles/op for 8 muls + 16 adds + 16 contiguous 64B-line stores per pair, already split by pair range; prepare's 0.156 ms = 37.4k cycles against ~20k ops of copy+memset+FWHT(6 groups x 7 stages x 64 butterflies)+scale pass = ~2 cycles/op. Both are at the scalar floor, and FWHT unroll is already a measured null, so the last two unpriced per-call costs in prep+lut are closed.
asi.state: every phase of the token now has a measured mechanism behind it; the request path reconciles at the 1 % level against per-call measurements (projection 0.23 ms, emit 0.10 ms), so the campaign's ~1 % bench-to-request residue is accounted and there is no unattributed budget left above the 0.2 % bar.
asi.next: attribute ND_P_ENGRAM (16.4 ms/token, 8.3 %, the largest phase not yet split per call) into gather vs its own 2-bit GEMVs vs conv, with the same per-call printf technique; the gather share is the only delivery-shaped mass in the map that the four gather closures (#340 tier, #341 n, #287 GDMA, #343 bit-width) did not directly measure.
asi.shipping_change: none - kbench.c is compiled only when NEEDLE_KBENCH is set, which no shipping configure does (run #330 verified the option branch is never evaluated); engine/ esp32/main/main.c unchanged

description: Benchmark-integrity + product-correctness iteration: widened held-out coverage found a real firmware defect, and two harness defects. Metric UNCHANGED at exactly 5.0300 - kept for correctness, not speed, stated plainly. ADDED three extended prompts the suite never measured (252-byte tools prompt whose answer is 132 tokens, 224-byte route prompt, schema's interval lower bound); host goldens re-saved with 16/16 pre-existing entries byte-identical. My first comparison reported all 16 as changed - that was my own json.dumps forgetting sort_keys on one side (key order, not content), same check-integrity family as #296/#300. DEFECT 1 FIRMWARE, FIXED: the device silently truncated every answer at 128 generated tokens - MAX_NEW was the only limit - so the 132-token answer came back as JSON cut mid-key (..."set_timer","arguments":{"seconds":300}},{"n ) and bench.py parsed calls=[] / BAD incomplete_call, while the same prompt on the host engine produced a valid 132-token list. A truncated tool call is worse than a slow one because nothing says it happened. Fix: MAX_NEW is now a 256 backstop, the real bound is the model's own remaining context (max_seq_len - pos, which also stops a long primed prefix walking pos past the trained context), and either stop now prints ERR generation_truncated produced= bytes= reason=. VERIFIED on device: the same case returns three well-formed calls, 51 tokens, 5.030 tps. All pre-existing goldens are <= 99 tokens, which is why 300+ runs never touched this. DEFECT 2 HARNESS, FIXED: bench.py formatted r['decode_tps'] with :.3f while aggregates used 'or 0.0', so the first case ever to see no EVT done killed the suite with a TypeError mid-run, costing a golden save and every case after it. DEFECT 3 OPEN: at 22 cases the last answers come back mis-paired (a route prompt answered with tools-schema calls, which the route grammar forbids) then WARN think ack missing + TimeoutError - run #155's abandoned-extended-set signature reproduced at a larger suite, so it is a session-lifetime defect, not my quoting. The device golden was NOT saved (bench.py saves at the end and the crash preceded it), so the three new cases still compare against nothing on device: the pairing fix must land first.

asi.candidate_tested_this_iteration: widened held-out coverage (3 new extended prompt shapes) - and the defect it immediately found: a hard 128-token generation cap in main.c silently truncating long tool calls into invalid JSON
asi.coverage_result: no overfitting signature needed - the new shapes found three defects instead. Model behaviour notes: 'Sample telemetry every second' resolves to seconds=120 (the same default the free-text and ambiguous cases produce, so the schema's lower bound is never selected by natural language); 40000 -> 400 is a clamp; both now recorded in prompts.json notes as behaviour, and my invented expect for the 1-second case was wrong and was removed rather than left to fail
asi.defect1_firmware: MAX_NEW=128 was the only generation limit -> 132-token answer truncated mid-JSON, parsed as calls=[] / BAD incomplete_call on device while host produced a valid list. Fixed: backstop 256, real bound max_seq_len - pos, explicit ERR generation_truncated. Device now returns 3 valid calls for that case, 51 tokens, tps 5.030.
asi.defect2_harness: bench.py f-string formatted None decode_tps -> TypeError killed the whole suite mid-run (the aggregate lines already used `or 0.0`)
asi.defect3_open: the last device answers are mis-paired with their prompts (a route prompt answered with tools-schema calls, which the route grammar forbids) then 'WARN think ack missing' + serial_api TimeoutError = run #155's signature reproduced at a larger suite. Note the 252-byte prompt is UNDER the firmware's 271-byte silent-truncation limit, so that is not the cause. Next: reproduce with primary,extended only and check whether serial_api.complete() can consume a stale END from a previous long response, and whether phase is applied before the write.
asi.hypothesis: extended had been watched for 200+ runs and is no longer held out; adding genuinely unseen shapes (long prefill, long route, interval lower bound) either shows an overfitting signature or finds behaviour the suite cannot see
asi.internal_heap_note: internal_free 14903 and psram_free 2052252 read from the EVT ready line of this very run, so the main.c fix costs no memory
asi.metric_meaning: 5.0300 is the unchanged accepted runtime: kept for a correctness fix with a metric-neutral measurement, not for a speed win
asi.next: fix the request/response pairing (likely an END drained from a previous response, or a phase applied after the write), then re-run AUTO_SAVE=1 to actually store the three device goldens, and re-read think_tps/boot bench which this crashed run never reached
asi.primary_metric_unaffected_by: the changed case is outside primary and no frozen generation exceeds 99 tokens; prefill moved 5.3067 -> 5.3083 (+0.03 % = one tick) and the boot bench was not re-measured because the run died in the think group
asi.secondary_provenance: prefill 5.3083, ext 4.9515 (13 cases), min_case 4.80, gen_tokens 99, internal_free 14903 and psram_free 2052252 (from this run's EVT ready line), host_output_exact 19/19 and device_output_exact 19/19 with zero DIVERGE/BAD lines are MEASURED this run; think_tps 3.94 and boot_bench 5.076 are carried from run #333 because the crashed run never reached the think group; fidelity 5.341e-05 / top1 10/10 come from the checks.sh that measure.sh ran and passed inside this run

description: Harness/session-pairing correctness iteration - the fix that #345 started, now COMPLETE and validated, no rerun and no coverage expansion. decode_tps stays exactly 5.0300 (+106.0 %): serial_api.py and bench.py are HOST-side bench dependencies that never enter the flashed image, so the shipping binary and its speed are unchanged by construction. The product is that the campaign's central gate (device byte-exactness) is now trustworthy on an enlarged suite. TWO DEFECTS FIXED. (1) RESPONSE PAIRING: the firmware has no request/response framing, so any line still queued when a request is written is read back as the start of THIS reply. bench.py runs the whole suite on one attach, so one extra/missing END shifts every later case by one - run #345's smoking gun was a route prompt answered with tools-schema calls its own grammar forbids. Fix: drain_stale() (drain-with-reads, since reset_input_buffer only clears bytes nobody has read yet) before every write in serial_api.complete(). VALIDATED on device: the same three prompts that came back swapped in #345 each answered their OWN schema here (long_route -> translate_or_write, interval_one -> set_sampling_interval, note_only -> set_sampling_interval), 20/20 byte-exact. (2) THINK-MODE ACK: after ~15-20 requests in one attached session the board stops answering !think (run #155's signature, reproduced #346: 27 stale lines drained and it STILL would not ack, so it is console fatigue, not backlog). Run #345 recorded think_tps=5.02 from a toggle that never took - a constrained-path number labelled as think. Fix: check the ack VALUE, and on a missing ack do one _reconnect()+_handshake() (clears the console without resetting the chip - DTR/RTS are pinned through the open - and re-establishes readiness), then fail loudly. MEASURED: WARN think ack missing -> reconnect -> METRIC think_tps=3.94, the correct unconstrained-vocabulary rate, matching history to the digit. Device golden saved and verified: 17 pre-existing entries carried over byte-identical, 3 added, 0 changed, 0 removed. TWO SELF-INFLICTED VARIANTS tried on real boards and REVERTED because they regressed: settle-to-quiet drain (quiet 1.5 s / budget 8 s) cut the suite to 17 cases + a request timeout vs 20/20 with a fixed 1 s window; and a fatal think-ack (SystemExit, no retry) aborted the canonical run instead of recovering. Both reasons are now code comments. Off-device falsification harness added (.auto/exp28/test_pairing.py, no board): drain counts 3-then-0, _set_think drains before writing, switch_think accepts a correct ack, rescues a wrong-then-right ack via reconnect, and raises THINK_ACK_MISSING only after exactly one reconnect - and it asserted-failed twice while I wrote it, which is the point. This was explicitly the preserve-and-log-once step the operator called for: no reruns, no further coverage expansion. Next action per the OPERATOR REDIRECT is three distinct performance lanes.

asi.candidate_tested_this_iteration: harness/session-pairing correctness: drain-before-write in serial_api (complete() and the !think toggle) + value-checked think ack with one no-reset reconnect retry + settle-to-quiet drain tried and rejected + fatal-ack abort tried and rejected
asi.defect_fixed_pairing: drain_stale() before every write. Without it one extra/missing END shifts EVERY later case by one; #345 measured a route prompt answered with tools-schema calls its grammar forbids. With the fixed-window drain, the same three prompts each answered their OWN schema (long_route->translate_or_write, interval_one->set_sampling_interval), and this run is 20/20 byte-exact.
asi.defect_fixed_think_ack: the !think ack value is now checked, and a missing ack triggers one _reconnect()+_handshake() (no chip reset, no re-prime) before failing loudly. Measured: WARN think ack missing -> reconnect -> METRIC think_tps=3.94, the correct constrained-vocabulary rate. Without this the suite either records a bogus 5.02 (run #345) or aborts (run #346 fatal ack).
asi.falsification: .auto/exp28/test_pairing.py drives both guards off-device: drain reports 3-then-0, _set_think drains before writing, switch_think accepts a correct ack, saves a wrong-then-right ack via the reconnect path, and fails THINK_ACK_MISSING only after exactly one reconnect. It asserted-failed twice while I wrote it, so it can actually fail.
asi.hypothesis: The mispairing and the missing think ack are console-backlog/session defects in the harness+bridge, not firmware inference faults. Test: drain the backlog before each write and reconnect (no reset) on a missing ack; if the board then acks think and every case answers its own schema, the hypothesis holds.
asi.lane_note: Board 1 stays the canonical board; this #346 was the single required preserve run. Boards 2/3 were idle and are now allocated to two NEW performance lanes; board 1 takes the third lane. The harness fix is stable and every candidate inherits it.
asi.next: Start three performance lanes within ten minutes per the OPERATOR REDIRECT: B1 fused/concurrent engram key+value CQ2 projections; B2 batched/interleaved Q/K/V/gate CQ2 projection scheduling across cores; B3 multi-row/two-stream CQ2 assembly schedule to hide PSRAM latency / amortize row overhead. Cheap real-byte kbench screens precede full runs. Dead lane replaced immediately.
asi.two_variants_rejected: settle-to-quiet drain (quiet 1.5s/budget 8s) REGRESSED the suite to 17 cases + a request timeout vs 20/20 with a fixed 1s window; and the fatal think-ack (SystemExit, no retry) aborted the canonical run. Both reverted, both reasons are code comments now.

description: Experiment 29 LANE 1 (board 1, kbench screen on real needle3.cact bytes, no shipping change - decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, kept so the bench asset survives): fusing the engram-like CQ2 pair - two 768x768 tensors that already share one prepared activation and one pair table - into a single nd_parallel_rows sweep over the concatenated row space is BIT-EXACT and worth +0.04 % (3,179,327 -> 3,178,074 cycles for 1,536 rows / 1,179,648 weights, min of 12 rounds, two-core, nd_lut2_rows_tie1n). A 64-row-block interleaved order is -0.03 %. Cycles per weight: shipping 2.6951, fused 2.6941, interleaved 2.6959. VERDICT reject: 0.04 % is well inside the campaign's measured 0.071 % three-identical-image board spread, and the mechanism the fusion was supposed to buy is already shipped - nd_model.c:1082-1102 does one nd_cq_prepare and one nd_cq_lut_build for the key/value pair, and run #344 measured the cross-core handshake at 23 cycles hot AND parked, so one job instead of two removes a cost that is not there. Two harness findings came out of this lane and both are fixed in the tree: (a) the first attempt printed asm=0 because ND_LUT2_ASM is a PRIVATE compile definition of the needle component and is therefore never visible inside kbench.c (which belongs to main), so guarding the kernel choice on it silently screens the C row walker and reports the wrong cost - the choice now follows nd_lut2_asm_ok() exactly as the shipping dispatcher does, and asm=1 confirms the TIE728 kernel ran; (b) my new integrity check reported bench_fused_in_elf=0 as if the candidate had not been compiled, but it had: it ran nm on elf_loader.elf instead of needle_demo.elf (the symbol is there and the map has .text.bench_fused) - fixed, and the console's own KB FUSE output remains the authority per #242.

asi.candidate: LANE 1 (board 1): fuse the engram-like pair - two 768x768 CQ2 tensors that already share one nd_cq_prepare + one nd_cq_lut_build - into ONE nd_parallel_rows sweep over the concatenated row space, instead of two per-tensor jobs. Also tested a 64-row-block interleaved order.
asi.closed_family: fused / concurrent / interleaved CQ2 projection scheduling. Both shapes measured on real bytes with the shipping kernel: 2-tensor pair +0.04 %/-0.03 %, 4-tensor q,k,v,gate +0.02 %/-0.08 % (lane 2, logged separately). The reason is now structural rather than guessed: nd_model.c:1464-1471 and :1082-1102 already share the prepare and the pair table, and run #344 measured the cross-core handshake at 23 cycles, so a fused job removes work that was never there.
asi.hypothesis: the engram key/value pair costs less as one sweep over both tensors' rows than as the shipping two sweeps, because the second sweep would start with the pair table, the activation and the tier pages already hot.
asi.kernel_provenance: asm=1 printed by the bench: nd_lut2_rows_tie1n, chosen by nd_lut2_asm_ok() exactly as the shipping dispatcher does. The first attempt (batch 0800L) printed asm=0 because ND_LUT2_ASM is a PRIVATE compile define of the needle component and so is never visible in kbench.c's translation unit - guarding on it silently screens the C walker and reports the wrong cost. Fixed by gating on nd_lut2_asm_ok() alone.
asi.integrity: bench_fused confirmed in the flashed app: xtensa-nm on needle_demo.elf has the symbol and the map has .text.bench_fused; the console printed KB FUSE lines, which is the authority (#242's rule). My first check reported bench_fused_in_elf=0 because it ran nm on elf_loader.elf; lane.sh now checks the app ELF.
asi.next: three new screens launched: tier LAYOUT permutation (four tensors contiguous in read order vs four allocations), attention Q.K operand reuse across positions, and cold-pass read-order sensitivity (ascending/descending/stride/random) which prices whether ANY layout permutation can pay.
asi.result: BIT-EXACT (mismatch=0 of 1536 rows) and +0.04 % for the fused single sweep; the row-block-interleaved order is -0.03 %. cycles/weight 2.6951 shipping vs 2.6941 fused vs 2.6959 interleaved, min of 12 rounds, two-core.
asi.verdict: REJECT. 0.04 % is 1/5 of the campaign's own 0.071 % three-board spread and a fifth of the 0.2 % keep bar, and the mechanism is already spent: the pair table is shared, the activation is shared, and the handshake is 23 cycles (run #344). Nothing shipped.

description: Experiment 29 LANE 2 (board 2, kbench, real archive bytes, no shipping change; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward): the operator's direction (B) - batch/interleave the independent Q/K/V/gate CQ2 projections across cores instead of paying sequential barriers - measured on the REAL row counts (576/96/128/768 x 768, one shared activation and pair table exactly as nd_model.c:1464-1471 already shares them). One fused nd_parallel_rows sweep over the concatenated 1,568-row space: +0.02 % (3,267,708 -> 3,267,149 cycles, 1,204,224 weights, 2.7135 -> 2.7131 cyc/weight, min of 12 rounds, two-core, nd_lut2_rows_tie1n, asm=1). A 64-row-block interleaved order: -0.08 % (2.7158). BIT-EXACT, mismatch = 0 of 1,568 rows. Verdict REJECT - with lane 1's +0.04 %/-0.03 % on the 768+768 engram pair this closes the fused/interleaved CQ2 scheduling family on measurement: the activation and pair table are already shared, the cross-core handshake is 23 cycles (#344), and every ordering variant lands inside the campaign's own 0.071 % three-board spread. My specific worry - that k(96) and v(128) give each core only 48/64 rows and so stream the tier badly - is answered by the fused sweep itself, which hands each core a contiguous 784-row half spanning all four tensors and changes nothing.

asi.candidate: LANE 2 (board 2): the real per-layer attention projection set q(576)+k(96)+v(128)+gate(768) rows, 768 columns, one activation and one pair table shared as shipping already shares them, measured (a) as the shipping four nd_parallel_rows jobs, (b) as one fused sweep over the concatenated row space, (c) as a 64-row-block interleaved order.
asi.changed_assumption: None invalidated. Lanes 1/2 are the operator's named directions (A) and (B) and both close on measurement, so no earlier discard needs revisiting: nothing here makes a previously rejected residency or clock idea cheaper.
asi.hypothesis: the small k(96) and v(128) tensors are the weak link: each half-split gives a core only 48/64 rows, so four sequential jobs may stream the PSRAM tier worse than one sweep over 1568 rows.
asi.next: the remaining lever for the 13.90 % cold PSRAM delivery tax is where the bytes ARE, not how they are called: (1) tier LAYOUT permutation - four CQ2 tensors contiguous in one buffer in per-token read order vs four allocations; (2) attention Q.K operand reuse across positions; (3) cold-pass read-order sensitivity (ascending/descending/stride/random), which prices whether ANY layout permutation can pay.
asi.result: 1,568 rows / 1,204,224 weights, bit-exact mismatch=0, min of 12 rounds, two-core, nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (asm=1): shipping four jobs 3,267,708 cycles (2.7135 cyc/weight), fused one sweep 3,267,149 (2.7131) = +0.02 %, 64-row interleaved 3,270,449 (2.7158) = -0.08 %.
asi.small_tensor_concern: tested and answered: if the 48-row and 64-row halves were the problem, the fused sweep - which gives each core a contiguous 784-row half across all four tensors - would have shown it. It shows 0.02 %, so small-job granularity is not a cost at 23-cycle handshakes.
asi.verdict: REJECT, and with lane 1 it closes the fused/interleaved CQ2 scheduling family (the operator's directions A and B) on measurement: the shared prepare and pair table are already shipped (nd_model.c:1464-1471, :1082-1102), the handshake is 23 cycles (#344), and every ordering variant lands inside the 0.071 % board spread.

description: Experiment 29 LANE 3 (board 3, kbench, real archive bytes, no shipping change; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward): the operator's direction (C) - does a multi-row / two-stream CQ2 schedule have anything to amortize? Priced with a rows-per-call curve instead of writing assembly first. One 768x768 CQ2 tensor (tensor 10, in_pad 768, row_bytes 192), shipping nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (asm=1), real needle3.cact bytes staged into PSRAM as the tier stages them, min of 12 rounds: cycles per output row = 2105.914 at 1 row/call, 2081.173 at 2, 2069.918 at 4, 2064.302 at 8, 2061.486 at 16 - total spread 2.16 %, marginal gain per doubling -1.17 %/-0.54 %/-0.27 %/-0.14 %, i.e. a converged curve with an asymptote around 2058 cyc/row. Verdict CLOSED without building: nd_parallel_rows already hands the kernel a contiguous [r0,r1) range, so the shipping call already sits at the far right of this curve; the 2.16 % belongs to a calling convention (one row per call) the firmware does not use, and the extrapolated benefit of a perfect two-row kernel is 0.17 % of the phase = +0.07 % decode, a third of the keep bar. This is the third independent confirmation that the dominant CQ2 phase is at its instruction floor: instruction count (2 per weight, #144-145), external clock (a 50 % wider MSPI moves the whole token 3.51 %, #289), and now per-row overhead (2.16 % from 1 to 16 rows, and 0.14 % over the last doubling).

asi.candidate: LANE 3 (board 3): the operator's direction (C) - a multi-row / two-stream CQ2 assembly schedule that hides PSRAM latency or amortizes row overhead. Priced before writing any assembly, by measuring the cost of one output row as a function of rows-per-call on the dominant 768x768 CQ2 tensor with the shipping kernel.
asi.converged_curve: 1->2 rows -1.17 %, 2->4 -0.54 %, 4->8 -0.27 %, 8->16 -0.14 %. Extrapolated asymptote ~2058 cyc/row, i.e. 0.17 % below the 16-row value. A perfect two-row kernel therefore buys <=0.17 % of proj2bit = 0.147 ms = +0.07 % decode, under a third of the keep bar. That is why no assembly was written: the measurement retires the design, not an opinion about it.
asi.hypothesis: row overhead per call is large enough that a multi-row / two-stream schedule could amortize it, which is the operator's direction (C) and the last unpriced structural idea for the dominant phase.
asi.invalidates_previous_discard: No. It strengthens the closures: the per-row cost curve is converged, so the two-row LUT blocking null (-5.1 %), the 4-row null (-5 %) and the ~25 scheduling nulls all sit where the curve says there is nothing left to amortize.
asi.next: layout, not scheduling: (1) four CQ2 tensors contiguous in ONE PSRAM buffer in per-token read order vs four allocations (the layout version of lanes 1/2, and the only untested way to change what the 13.90 % cold tax is paying for); (2) attention Q.K operand reuse across positions (q held over K rows) - 8.3 ms of dots is the largest non-GEMV mass; (3) cold-pass read-order sensitivity (ascending / descending / stride 4/16/64 / random) which prices whether ANY permutation of bytes can pay, gating (1)'s family.
asi.result: cyc/row for one 768x768 CQ2 tensor, nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (asm=1), real archive bytes, min of 12 rounds: rows/call 1 = 2105.914, 2 = 2081.173, 4 = 2069.918, 8 = 2064.302, 16 = 2061.486. Total spread 2.16 %, and the marginal gain per doubling collapses -1.17 % / -0.54 % / -0.27 % / -0.14 %, i.e. a converged curve.
asi.shipping_already_amortized: nd_parallel_rows hands the kernel a contiguous [r0,r1) range, so the shipping call is already the far right of the curve (~384 rows per core). The 2.16 % is the cost of the WORST possible calling convention, not a budget a new kernel can collect.
asi.verdict: REJECT / CLOSED before building: the amortization prize is 0 %, because shipping already passes ranges, and even the un-collectable 2.16 % of proj2bit (86.2 ms) would be 1.9 ms = +0.94 % only if the kernel were calling once per row, which it is not.

description: Experiment 30 LANE 1 (board 1, kbench, real archive bytes; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward - no shipping change): TIER LAYOUT, the lever left after Experiment 29 closed scheduling. Laying the four attention CQ2 tensors' bytes (576/96/128/768 x 768, 319,872 B) out contiguously in per-token read order instead of four separate allocations is BIT-EXACT (mismatch = 0 of 1,568 rows - same bytes, different addresses) and worth **+0.89 %** on the dominant two-core pass: 3,267,790 -> 3,238,852 cycles, 2.7136 -> 2.6896 cycles/weight, min of 12 rounds, shipping nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (asm=1). Against proj2bit = 86.2 ms of a 197 ms token that is 0.77 ms/token = **+0.39 % decode**, above the 0.2 % keep bar, and it is the strongest candidate since run #333. It is NOT integrated, because my baseline is not shipping's layout: nd_tier_ptr maps one contiguous archive span 1:1 into the 12 MB tier, so a layer's q/k/v/gate are already adjacent in PSRAM, and a packed tier needs a per-tensor offset map. The screen therefore measures 'scattered mallocs -> packed', an upper bound on 'archive-offset span -> packed'. Lane 3 independently confirms the mechanism is real: on a cold pass over one tensor, ascending (what the model does) is best at 2.7471 cyc/weight and shuffled is +6.35 % worse, with descending +1.10 % and stride-4 +3.08 % in between. Next measurement is the integration gate: packed vs a shipping-like archive-offset layout inside one buffer.

asi.correct_next_measurement: Before integrating anything: re-run the comparison against a SHIPPING-LIKE layout - one big buffer with each tensor memcpy'd at (archive_off - region_lo), which is what nd_tier_ptr's 1:1 mapping actually produces - vs the packed use-ordered buffer. That is the apples-to-apples test, and it is the first lane of the next batch. Recorded as a caveat rather than shipped because shipping's four attention tensors are adjacent in the archive, so the tier may already be effectively packed for them.
asi.hypothesis: the 12 MB tier copies a raw archive SPAN, so a token's CQ2 reads are spread over megabytes of address space; packing the same bytes contiguously in per-token read order should reduce the address space walked per token and cut part of the measured flat 13.90 % cold PSRAM delivery tax (#330).
asi.invalidates_previous_discard: Potentially run #340 (embedding reads through the tier, +0.03 %) - but no: #340 changed WHICH pointer a scattered gather used, not the layout of the bytes, so its null stands. It does reopen the TIER family, which the ledger had closed on span/stride/copy-order/coverage: those knobs all preserve the 1:1 archive-to-PSRAM mapping, and layout permutation is a different lever that was never in the family.
asi.lane3_independent_confirmation: order does matter on cold passes over one tensor: ascending 2.7471 cyc/weight, descending 2.7773 (+1.10 %), stride4 2.8316 (+3.08 %), stride16 2.7831, stride64 2.7516, shuffled 2.9214 (+6.35 %). Ascending - what the model already does per tensor - is the best of six, which both bounds the win (a token's real order is already near-best within a tensor) and proves address order is a real ~6 % lever on this phase, not noise.
asi.next: next batch: (A) packed vs shipping-like archive-offset layout in one buffer (the integration gate for this result); (B) attention P.V accumulate loop interchange - the biggest unmeasured sub-block of the 35.3 ms head split, bit-exact by construction because every oh cell accumulates independently; (C) TIE wide-load FWHT in nd_cq_prepare, where wide float loads on plain aligned floats are unaffected by #335's nibble-identity defect.
asi.result: 1,568 rows / 1,204,224 weights, mismatch = 0 (bit-exact by construction: identical bytes at different addresses), min of 12 rounds, two-core, nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (asm=1). Four heap allocations spread over PSRAM: 3,267,790 cycles (2.7136 cyc/weight). Same bytes packed into one 319,872 B buffer in per-token read order: 3,238,852 cycles (2.6896) = +0.89 %.
asi.screen: kbench on board 1, real needle3.cact bytes staged into PSRAM as the tier stages them. decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward - no shipping change, this is a screen.
asi.strongest_candidate: Since run #333's phi asm (+0.365 %). 0.89 % of proj2bit (86.2 ms) is 0.77 ms/token = +0.39 % decode at the campaign's measured 25-70 % realisation band.
asi.verdict: NOT integrated yet, deliberately, and the reason is a real mismatch in my own baseline: layout A in this screen was four separate heap_caps_malloc blobs, but shipping does NOT do that - nd_tier_ptr maps a single contiguous archive span 1:1 (return m->eg_vpsram + (t->offset - m->eg_region_lo)), so a layer's q/k/v/gate already sit adjacent in PSRAM at their archive offsets. The +0.89 % therefore measures 'scattered mallocs -> packed', which is an UPPER bound on 'archive-offset span -> packed'.

description: Experiment 30 LANE 2 (board 2, kbench; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, no shipping change): attention Q.K operand reuse. Measured the shipped two-term-group dot (dot_c4 schedule) on n=48 vectors, 256 dots/round, min of 25 rounds: both operands rotating (the shipping loop's shape) 229.93 cycles/dot, q fixed for the whole inner block 226.80 = +1.38 %. Taking +1.38 % as the ceiling for keeping q live across positions of a head, the prize is 1.38 % of 8.3 ms = 0.115 ms/token = +0.06 % decode, under a third of the keep bar, so the head loop is not restructured. Two honesty notes recorded in the bench output: my two-positions-per-q variant compared its accumulated total against a single pair's scalar sum (pair_vs_scalar_mismatch=3 of 4 - my comparison was wrong, not the schedule), and both variants are pure over global arrays, which is exactly run #230's recorded hoisting trap, so the absolute cycles are an upper bound rather than a clean schedule measurement. Closed on the bound because even the bound is below the bar.

asi.candidate: LANE 2 (board 2): attention Q.K operand reuse - the shipped loop hands the dot a fresh q and a fresh k each position, but q is invariant across the positions of one head, so keeping it live is operand reuse (#230 tested interleaving and extra accumulators, never reuse).
asi.harness_defect_found: kb_dot_q2 compared its accumulated total against one pair's scalar sum, so pair_vs_scalar_mismatch=3 of 4 is MY comparison being wrong, not the schedule; and both helper variants are pure over global arrays, which is #230's documented hoisting trap (a fixed-operand pure call gets lifted out of the timing loop). Both make lane 2's absolute numbers untrustworthy. Closed on the upper bound instead of re-running, because even the ceiling is under the bar; the pair form must be re-tested with rotated per-iteration operands and a per-iteration consume if it is ever revisited.
asi.hypothesis: ~14,400 dots x 138 cycles = 8.3 ms of the attention stage; if a resident q made each dot cheaper, restructuring the head loop to hold q live across positions would pay.
asi.next: not this - the next batch is (A) the packed-vs-archive-offset layout gate for lane 1's +0.89 %, (B) the attention P.V accumulate loop interchange, which is the biggest unmeasured sub-block of the 35.3 ms head split and is bit-exact by construction because every oh cell accumulates independently, (C) TIE wide-load FWHT in nd_cq_prepare.
asi.result: both operands rotating (the shipping shape) 229.93 cycles/dot; q fixed for the inner block 226.80 = +1.38 %. Taking that as the CEILING for keeping q resident: 1.38 % of 8.3 ms = 0.115 ms/token = +0.06 % decode, under a third of the 0.2 % keep bar.
asi.verdict: REJECT on an upper bound. A +1.4 % operand-reuse win on an 8.3 ms phase is 0.06 % of the token, so no head-loop restructuring is warranted even if the schedule were perfect. The same arithmetic is why the campaign keeps landing on phases, not micro-schedules: at 197 ms/token, only phases above ~5 ms can pay a 0.2 % candidate.

description: Experiment 30 LANE 3 (board 3, kbench, real archive bytes; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, no shipping change): cold-pass read-order sensitivity, the cheap gate for the byte-layout family. One 768x768 CQ2 tensor (589,824 weights), shipping nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (asm=1), 160 KB PSRAM sweep before every timed pass to evict the 64 KB data cache, min of 10 rounds: cycles/weight 2.7471 ascending, 2.7773 descending (+1.10 %), 2.8316 stride-4 (+3.08 %), 2.7831 stride-16 (+1.31 %), 2.7516 stride-64 (+0.16 %), 2.9214 shuffled (+6.35 %). Two conclusions: the answer is NOT flat, so address order is a genuine ~6 % lever on the dominant phase - which is independent physical confirmation of the mechanism run #350 measured from the other side; and ascending, which is exactly what the model already does inside a tensor, is the best of the six, so no headroom remains within a tensor and the only remaining question is inter-tensor placement, i.e. what the tier's 1:1 archive-span mapping does. Recording also that my own summary line printed the spread with the wrong sign (-5.97 % where the reading is 'shuffled is 6.35 % worse'); the per-order lines are the authority.

asi.candidate: LANE 3 (board 3): cold-pass read-order sensitivity of the dominant CQ2 tensor - ascending, descending, stride 4/16/64, and Fisher-Yates shuffled visits over one 768x768 tensor, with a 160 KB PSRAM sweep evicting the data cache before each timed pass. This is the cheap gate that decides whether ANY byte-layout permutation can pay, which is the family run #350's +0.89 % belongs to.
asi.hypothesis: if cycles/weight were flat across visit orders, no layout permutation could pay and the whole tier-layout family would close off-device; if not flat, the spread is the budget a layout change can spend.
asi.numbers: asc 2.7471 / desc 2.7773 (+1.10 %) / stride4 2.8316 (+3.08 %) / stride16 2.7831 (+1.31 %) / stride64 2.7516 (+0.16 %) / shuffled 2.9214 (+6.35 %) cyc per weight; 589,824 weights per pass, min of 10 rounds, nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (asm=1), cold by construction.
asi.note_on_printed_spread: the bench's own order_spread line printed -5.97 % because it divided asc by shuffled and reported it as a signed spread; the magnitudes above are the correct reading (shuffled is 6.35 % WORSE than ascending). Fixed in the bench's follow-up so a future reader is not misled by the sign.
asi.result: NOT flat: ascending (which is what the model already does per tensor) is the BEST of six orders at 2.7471 cyc/weight; descending +1.10 %, stride-4 +3.08 %, stride-16 +1.31 %, stride-64 +0.16 %, shuffled +6.35 %. So address order is a real ~6 % lever on the dominant phase, and the model's within-tensor order is already at the optimum.
asi.verdict: Family stays OPEN but the budget is bounded and the shipping order is already best-in-class within a tensor: the only headroom left is BETWEEN tensors, i.e. how the tier places different tensors relative to each other, which is exactly run #350's measurement. Two independent results (#350's +0.89 % packed-vs-scattered, and this 6.35 % ascending-vs-shuffled) now say the delivery tax has a layout component; whether the shipping 1:1 span mapping already collects it is the next measurement.

description: Experiment 31 LANE 1 (board 1, kbench, real archive bytes; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, no shipping change): the integration gate on the byte-layout lever, and it says do not build it. Comparing shipping's actual tier mapping (one buffer, each tensor at archive_off - region_lo, exactly what nd_tier_ptr computes) against the same bytes packed at 64 B-aligned offsets in per-token read order: shipping 3,270,319 cycles vs packed 3,299,493 for 1,204,224 weights = packing is **0.88 % WORSE** (2.7157 vs 2.7399 cyc/weight), bit-exact mismatch=0 of 1,568 rows, min of 14 rounds, nd_lut2_rows_tie1n. So run #350's +0.89 % was entirely 'four scattered heap allocations -> packed', a comparison against a baseline shipping does not have. The gap table explains why packing cannot win here: the archive puts 537 KB between q and k and 537 KB between k and v, and gate's offset sits 375 KB *before* v, so the read order is not an address order either. Byte-layout family CLOSED on three measurements (#350 packed-vs-scattered +0.89 %, this packed-vs-shipping-map -0.88 %, #351 within-tensor order ascending already best) and an integration that would have measured -0.9 % was avoided for the price of one screen.

asi.candidate: LANE 1 (board 1): the integration gate for run #350's +0.89 %. Layout A = one PSRAM buffer with each tensor at (archive_off - min_off), which is exactly the mapping nd_tier_ptr implements; layout B = the same bytes packed at 64 B-aligned offsets in per-token read order, in its own buffer. Bit-exact by construction, so any delta is placement.
asi.hypothesis: run #350's packed-vs-scattered-mallocs +0.89 % might transfer to the shipping tier. It does not, and the reason is visible in the gap table: the archive does NOT place q/k/v/gate contiguously (gap_before = 537,472 B twice), so the 1:1 span mapping already spreads them - and it still wins.
asi.mechanism_note: The archive gap table (537 KB between q and k, 537 KB between k and v, and a NEGATIVE -375,744 for gate, i.e. gate's bytes overlap the span between k and v in offset order) shows the four tensors are not in read order in the archive either. So neither packing nor reordering is available for free, and the shipping mapping is still the faster of the two measured.
asi.next: the FWHT. 31C found the transform owns 64.1 % of nd_cq_prepare = ~2.5 ms/token at 14 cycles/butterfly against a ~6-instruction body. Experiment 32 lane 1 screens scalar/unroll/block4/wide-load variants behind a known-answer probe. IMPORTANT finding already measured before that batch: FLOAT SIMD DOES NOT EXIST on this part - ee.add.64, ee.adds.64, ee.adds.sp, ee.addsp.64, ee.vadd.64, ee.sub*.64, ee.mul*.64 and ee.ldf.32 are all rejected by the shipped assembler ('unknown opcode or format name'), which independently confirms what engine/src/lut2_tie728.S:24 records. Only wide float LOADS assemble, and #335 showed they can return wrong values. So a vectorised FWHT is impossible; the remaining lever is fewer load/store instructions per butterfly.
asi.result: shipping 1:1 tier map 3,270,319 cycles (2.7157 cyc/weight); packed use-ordered 3,299,493 (2.7399) => packing is 0.88 % WORSE, bit-exact (mismatch=0 of 1,568), min of 14 rounds, nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (asm=1). Archive gap table: q id=2 off=3256704 nb=117504 gap=0; k id=30 off=3911680 nb=19584 gap=537472; v id=58 off=4468736 nb=26112 gap=537472; gate id=38 off=4119104 nb=156672 gap=-375744.
asi.verdict: LAYOUT FAMILY CLOSED, and an integration was avoided. The tier's 1:1 archive-span mapping is already the better of the two layouts, so there is no packed-tier candidate to build: run #350's +0.89 % was measuring 'scattered heap allocations -> packed', which shipping never does. This is exactly what the gate was for - the alternative was shipping a change that would have measured about -0.9 %.

description: Experiment 31 LANE 2 (board 2, kbench; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, no shipping change): the attention P.V accumulate order. Shipped position-major read-modify-write 9.587 cycles per output update vs a dim-major chunked form 17.164 cycles/update => the chunked form is 44.1 % WORSE, and the reordering was verified bit-exact first (order_mismatch = 0 of 192 cells, 6,144 updates). REJECT/CLOSED: the shipped order is nowhere near the bad alternative, so there is no accumulate-order lever in the head split. The useful by-product is the first measured cost of the P.V update itself - 9.59 cycles per cell - which says the ~15 ms attributed to it is real scalar work, not slack, consistent with the ledger's kron_apply lesson that reuse has to come from the operand loaded per cell.

asi.candidate: LANE 2 (board 2): the attention P.V accumulate, dim-major (chunked) vs the shipped position-major read-modify-write of the output rows, verified cell-by-cell first.
asi.hypothesis: the P.V accumulate is the largest unmeasured sub-block of the 35.3 ms head split (~15 ms/token by subtraction of the measured dot and exp costs), and its shipped form walks the output row per position, re-reading and re-writing memory per cell. Chunking dim-major should reuse a weight across positions.
asi.result: shipped position-major 58,904 cycles for 6,144 updates = 9.587 cycles/update; dim-major chunked 105,455 cycles = 17.164 cycles/update => the chunked form is 44.1 % WORSE. Bit-exact: order_mismatch = 0 of 192 cells.
asi.why: in the shipped order a whole output row stays hot and the weight is a register; dim-major makes the inner stride 24 floats and re-walks the K-position weight vector per column. This is the same shape of result as the ledger's kron_apply finding - reuse must come from the operand that is actually loaded per cell, not from accumulator arrangement.
asi.verdict: REJECT and CLOSED: the shipped form is far from the worst alternative, so there is no accumulate-order lever. The by-product number is worth having - P.V costs 9.59 cycles per output update on this core, which means the 15 ms attributed to it is ~3.6M updates/token of real work at the scalar floor, not slack.
asi.next: E32 lane 1 screens the FWHT (64.1 % of prepare per 31C). E32 lane 2 prices the engine's own nd_cq_prepare at each real geometry so the FWHT prize has a real denominator. E32 lane 3 screens the scale pass, which 31C measured at 11.1 cycles per element - far off a multiply, so it may have a restrict/unroll lever worth 14.5 % of a 3.9 ms/token phase.
asi.isa_finding: float SIMD arithmetic does not exist on this part: ee.add.64 / ee.adds.64 / ee.adds.sp / ee.addsp.64 / ee.vadd.64 / ee.sub*.64 / ee.mul*.64 / ee.ldf.32 are all rejected by the shipped assembler as 'unknown opcode or format name'. Only wide float loads (ee.ldf.64.ip, ee.ldf.128.ip) assemble. So a vectorised FWHT or vectorised scale is impossible; E32 was rewritten around legal forms before it ever reached a board.

description: Experiment 31 LANE 3 (board 3, kbench; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, no shipping change): nd_cq_prepare split for the first time, on the real geometry (in_pad 768, ngroup 6, group 128). Per call: activation copy 1,954 cycles (3.3 %), FWHT 37,763 (64.1 %), scale pass 8,519 (14.5 %), whole engine call 58,901 cycles = 0.2454 ms. At ~16 calls/token the transform is ~2.5 ms of the 197 ms token and the whole call reproduces the phase map's prep+lut (3.6 ms), which cross-checks the split against an independent measurement. Two disclosures: (1) my own summary line printed the call time in seconds under a 'ms' label and therefore read '0.000 ms' - the cycles are right, the units in that one line were wrong, and the correct reading is 0.2454 ms/call and 3.93 ms/token; this is the same unit/normalisation class that produced the retired 5.7 ms projection figure (#341) and the wrong-signed spread (#351), so the campaign rule is to trust the per-field numbers and re-derive any summary. (2) The scale pass costs 11.1 cycles per element, which is far off a multiply, so it has its own small lever (ceiling +0.29 %). The keepable-looking finding is the transform: 64.1 % of prepare at 14 cycles per butterfly against a ~6-instruction body, so a 2x transform is ~1.26 ms = +0.64 % decode. That is the prize Experiment 32 is screening - and a vector form of it is already impossible on an ISA fact (no float SIMD arithmetic assembles on this part).

asi.candidate: LANE 3 (board 3): split nd_cq_prepare into copy / +FWHT / +scale / whole engine call, all timed in one image on the real tensor geometry (in_pad 768, ngroup 6, group 128). Run #344 priced the whole call at 0.156 ms and ~2 cycles/op but never split it, so the TIE-FWHT idea had no denominator.
asi.harness_defect_disclosed: my own VERDICT line printed best[3]/240e6 (SECONDS) under a 'ms' label, so it read '0.000 ms call' and '0.00 ms'. The cycles are right and the correct figures are 0.2454 ms per call and 3.93 ms of FWHT+scale+copy per token across ~16 calls. The campaign's standing rule applies: the per-field numbers are the authority, and the derived summary line is the thing to re-check - this is the same class of unit/normalisation error that produced the retired 5.7 ms projection figure in #341 and the wrong-signed spread in #351.
asi.hypothesis: prepare's 0.156-0.245 ms per call, ~16 times a token, is 3.6 ms of the phase map's prep+lut; whether the transform is the majority decides if a vectorised FWHT is worth designing at all.
asi.result: copy 1,954 cycles (3.3 % of the call), FWHT 37,763 (64.1 %), scale 8,519 (14.5 %), whole engine call 58,901 cycles = 0.2454 ms. Sum of my three stages is 48,236, so the engine's own version carries ~18 % more (padding/memset and the fp16 staging the engine does around them). 16 calls/token reproduces prep+lut = 3.6-3.9 ms.
asi.scale_pass_finding: 8,519 cycles for 768 multiplies is 11.1 cycles per element, which is far off a multiply's floor and is why E32 lane 3 screens restrict/unroll forms of it. Its ceiling is 14.5 % of a 3.9 ms/token phase, so even making it free is +0.29 %, and halving it is +0.145 % - a real but small lever.
asi.verdict: KEEP as attribution, no candidate on its own: the FWHT is 64.1 % of prepare, ~2.5 ms/token, at 14 cycles per butterfly against a ~6-instruction body. That is the first above-bar-looking target found since the phi asm, and it is what Experiment 32 is screening.
asi.next: E32 lane 1 = scalar vs unroll vs block4 vs wide-load-fed scalar butterfly, behind the delta/constant known-answer probe; lane 2 = does my model FWHT match nd_cq_prepare bit-for-bit, and the engine call's real cost per geometry; lane 3 = the scale pass forms. The vector form is off the table on an ISA fact, not an opinion.
asi.unit_correction: FWHT = 37,763 cyc/call x 16 calls = 604,208 cycles = 2.52 ms/token; at 14 cycles/butterfly a 2x faster transform is ~1.26 ms = +0.64 % decode, which is 3 keep bars - that is the prize being screened, stated with the corrected units.

description: Experiment 32 LANE 1 (board 1, kbench; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, no shipping change): the FWHT screen, and the wide-load form wins on the kernel while the ISA closes the door on the version everyone would have reached for first. Float SIMD arithmetic DOES NOT EXIST on this part — ee.add.64, ee.adds.64, ee.adds.sp, ee.addsp.64, ee.vadd.64, ee.sub*.64, ee.mul*.64 and ee.ldf.32 are all rejected by the shipped assembler as "unknown opcode or format name" (which independently confirms what engine/src/lut2_tie728.S:24 already records), so a vectorised transform is impossible. What IS legal is the same scalar add.s/sub.s fed by wide TIE loads: **145,107 cycles scalar vs 122,162 with ee.ldf.64.ip/ee.stf.64.ip = +18.78 %**, unroll-2 +16.23 %, 4-butterfly register block -0.30 %, all bit-exact (diff 0) and all passing the known-answer probe (probe_bad=0). The transform is 64.1 % of prepare = ~2.52 ms/token, so the prize is ~0.40 ms = +0.20 % decode — exactly the keep bar, which is why it must now be measured through the real two-core call rather than priced here. Second-order finding with wider reach: **wide TIE float loads are trustworthy on plain aligned fp32 arrays**, so run #335's wrong-value defect is specific to the 2-bit decoder pattern, not to ee.ldf — that widens which kernels can use them. Honesty limit: this lane's reference was my own reconstruction, and lane 2 proves it is not bit-equal to the engine's output, so the bit-exactness claim here is relative to my model; Experiment 33 re-diffs every variant against the shipped nd_fwht symbol before anything is integrated.

asi.candidate: LANE 1 (board 1, kbench): four forms of the butterfly loop that dominates nd_cq_prepare, timed on the real group geometry (6 groups x g=128 = 2,688 butterflies per round), all diffed cell-by-cell. Variants: scalar control, k-loop unroll-2, 4-butterfly register block, and the SAME scalar add.s/sub.s fed by ee.ldf.64.ip wide loads + ee.stf.64.ip wide stores.
asi.hypothesis: run #351 measured the transform at 64.1 % of nd_cq_prepare (~2.5 ms/token) at 14 cycles per butterfly against a ~6-instruction body, so the transform has ~2x of headroom. A float-SIMD version is impossible (measured: ee.add.64 / ee.adds.64 / ee.sub*.64 / ee.mul*.64 / ee.ldf.32 are all rejected by the shipped assembler), so the question is whether fewer load/store instructions around the same scalar arithmetic pays.
asi.result: cycles per round: scalar 145,107 (13.50 cyc/butterfly), unroll2 124,850 (11.61) = +16.23 %, block4 145,539 (13.54) = -0.30 %, wide_load64 122,162 (11.36) = +18.78 %. diff_vs_scalar = 0,0,0,0 and the known-answer probe is clean for every variant (probe_bad=0,0,0,0), so all four compute identical bits.
asi.scope_correction: The reference in THIS lane was my own reconstruction of the transform, not the engine's. Run #357 (this batch's lane 2) shows the reconstruction is not bit-equal to what nd_cq_prepare produces (762 of 768 cells differ), so this lane's cycles-per-butterfly is a valid kernel comparison but its 'bit-exact' claim is only relative to my model. That is why nothing here is treated as an integration licence and Experiment 33 re-diffs every variant against the SHIPPED nd_fwht symbol.
asi.isa_finding: wide TIE float loads ARE trustworthy for plain aligned fp32 arrays: ee.ldf.64.ip/ee.stf.64.ip passed both the bit-differential and the known-answer probe here, so run #335's wrong-value defect is specific to the 2-bit decoder access pattern, not to the instruction. That widens what is buildable: wide loads can be used in float kernels as long as the differential says so.
asi.verdict: SCREEN ONLY, no candidate yet: the winner is the wide-load form at +18.78 %, worth 2.52 ms x 0.158 = 0.40 ms/token = +0.20 % decode at best, which is exactly the keep bar, so it must be measured end to end through the real two-core call, not priced from this screen.
asi.next: E33 lane 3 is that measurement (whole prepare, two-core, against nd_cq_prepare itself). If it shows >=13 % on the call with zero mismatches, integrate both changes (wide-load butterflies + unroll-4 rescale) and run the canonical pipeline; otherwise the family closes at screen level.

description: Experiment 32 LANE 2 (board 2, kbench; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, no shipping change): the denominator for the prepare family, and a self-correction. nd_cq_prepare costs **58,902 cycles = 0.2454 ms at every geometry** (three 768x768 tensors and one 576x768, all in_pad 768 / ngroup 6) — independent of row count exactly as the code says it must be, so ~16 calls/token = 3.93 ms = 2 % of the token, and run #344's 0.156 ms figure is superseded (that was one core's share, not the two-core wall time this runs on). The correction: my reconstructed transform differs from the engine's output on **762 of 768 cells**, because the engine rescales each group by 1/sqrtf(g) inside fwht_rows while my model scaled once by 1/n. So run #351's 64.1 % / 14.5 % split describes MY transform, not the shipped one — the qualitative shape holds (transform dominant, scale minority, copy noise) but the percentages are not the engine's. Disclosed alongside: my own 'model_ms' field is derived from the engine's cycles, not an independent measurement, so it must not be read as two agreeing measurements. This is why Experiment 33 diffs every variant against the shipped nd_fwht symbol rather than a transcription — the rule run #338 learned, applied.

asi.candidate: LANE 2 (board 2, kbench): nd_cq_prepare timed per real tensor geometry, and my reconstructed transform diffed cell-by-cell against what the engine actually writes.
asi.hypothesis: the FWHT prize needs a real denominator. Run #344 priced the call at 0.156 ms and run #351 at 0.2454 ms; if prepare's cost depended on the tensor's row count, one phase-map figure could not be used for all ~16 calls per token.
asi.result: engine call = 58,902 cycles = 0.2454 ms at every geometry tested (three 768x768 tensors and one 576x768, all in_pad=768, ngroup=6). It is independent of out rows exactly as the code says it must be (prepare touches only the activation), so 0.2454 ms is the correct per-call denominator for the whole family, and run #344's 0.156 ms is superseded - it measured one core's share, not the two-core wall time.
asi.model_mismatch: model_vs_engine_bad = 762, 762, 764, 764 of 768 cells: my reconstruction is NOT what the engine produces, because the engine rescales each group by 1/sqrtf(g) inside fwht_rows while my model applied 1/n once at the end. So the 64.1 %/14.5 % split from run #351 came from a transform+scale that is not the shipped one, and the safe reading is: the split's SHAPE (transform dominates, scale is a minority, copy is noise) is right, but the exact percentages are my model's, not the engine's.
asi.correction: the 'model_ms=0.2454' field in my own output line is derived from the engine's cycles, not an independent measurement of my model - do not read it as agreement between two measurements. There is one measurement here (58,902 cycles) and one comparison (762/768 mismatch).
asi.verdict: KEEP as the denominator plus a correction: prepare is 0.2454 ms per call and ~16 calls/token = 3.93 ms = 2 % of the token, and no candidate may be priced off my reconstructed transform. This is what forced Experiment 33 to re-diff every variant against the shipped nd_fwht symbol instead of against a transcription (run #338's rule, applied).

description: Experiment 32 LANE 3 (board 3, kbench; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, no shipping change): the per-group rescale inside fwht_rows. Shipped scalar loop 5,381 cycles for 768 elements = 7.01 cyc/element; **restrict-qualified: 5,381 cycles, identical, literally zero effect**; unroll-4: 2,896 = 3.77 cyc/element = **+85.81 %**, bit-exact (scale_mismatch=0 — each element is its own multiply, there is no accumulation order to move). Two things come out of it. (1) Another restrict null, and this one kills the backlog's cheapest suggestion — "add restrict to the hot elementwise kernels (zero numerical change)" — on measurement rather than assumption: the compiler already had the alias information the annotation supplies, exactly as in the earlier rms_unit/zcrms nulls. (2) A premise correction that shrinks the prize honestly: run #351's 11.1 cyc/element came from my reconstructed transform (see run #357), and the shipped-style loop measured in isolation is 7.01, so unroll-4 saves 3.14 cyc x 768 x ~16 calls = 0.16 ms/token = **+0.08 %**, under the keep bar alone. It is therefore bundled into the same patch as the transform instead of shipped by itself — worth taking, not worth a build.

asi.candidate: LANE 3 (board 3, kbench): the per-group rescale that fwht_rows runs after the transform (nd_quant.c: 'for (j = 0; j < c->g; j++) blk[j] *= c->scale;'), shipped form vs restrict-qualified vs unroll-4, on an aligned 768-float internal-RAM array, diffed bit-for-bit.
asi.hypothesis: run #351 measured the rescale at 11.1 cycles per element, which is nowhere near a multiply's floor, so it may have a lever worth 14.5 % of a 2 % phase.
asi.result: 768 elements: shipped 5,381 cycles = 7.01 cyc/element, restrict-qualified 5,381 = **identical, zero effect**, unroll-4 2,896 = 3.77 cyc/element = **+85.81 %**. scale_mismatch=0, so unroll-4 is bit-exact (each element is its own multiply; no ordering to move).
asi.second_restrict_null: this is the campaign's Nth restrict null - the ledger already records restrict on rms_unit/zcrms as a null, and the compiler's own alias analysis already had the information the annotation gives. Recorded because it kills 'add restrict to the hot elementwise kernels', the backlog's cheapest suggested idea, for one board run.
asi.note: the 11.1 cyc/element premise was my reconstructed model's number (see run #357); the shipped-style loop measured in isolation here is 7.01, so the lever is smaller than the model implied: unroll-4 saves 3.14 cycles x 768 x 16 calls/token = 38.6k cycles = 0.16 ms = +0.08 % on its own, i.e. below the bar alone and only worth taking as part of the same patch as the transform.
asi.verdict: KEEP as a component: unroll-4 on the rescale is free, bit-exact and worth +0.08 % alone; it is bundled into the E33 lane-3 candidate rather than shipped separately, because 0.08 % cannot clear the bar on its own.
asi.next: harvest E33: lane 1 (variants vs the SHIPPED nd_fwht), lane 2 (rescale forms at the engine's g=128), lane 3 (whole two-core prepare body both ways vs nd_cq_prepare's own output). If lane 3 shows >=13 % with zero mismatches, patch nd_fwht + fwht_rows and run the canonical three-board batch.

description: Harness iteration (no measurement; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward): **why two full three-board Experiment-33 batches were worthless, and the hole that made them look healthy.** The flashed images contained bench_e32/bench_fused and none of the E33 code, yet build_rc=0, flash_rc=0, the board booted, ran a *complete* bench sequence and printed EVT KBENCH_DONE. Root cause: esp32/main/CMakeLists.txt forwarded ND_KB_EXP30/31/32 to the compiler but **not ND_KB_EXP33** (each experiment's two lines had been hand-copied), so `-DND_KB_EXP33=1` sat unused in the CMake cache, the macro compiled as 0 and the dispatch silently fell through to the old default body. Every check passed because none of them asked the one question that mattered: build rc can't fail (an uncalled static function never fails to link), the lane macro really was on the compile line, and the ELF probe printed the informative `0` under a label that still said `bench_fused_in_elf`, so it read as the known #347 nm false alarm. Found three more holes while fixing it: (2) lane.sh built the build-dir name from EXP30/31/32 only, so an EXP33 build reused the all-zero `build-e29-000-1` directory — the stale-CMakeCache trap the ledger already records twice; (3) a genuine memory-corruption bug in the untested wide-load variant: `kb_fwht_u2ld2` reused one C pointer as both the load and store cursor, and because `ee.ldf.64.ip` post-updates its base register, the stores wrote **16 bytes past** the butterflies just read — found by reading the asm, not by running it, and it would have corrupted exactly the two lanes that use it. Fixes kept: a `foreach(kb_exp 30..36)` forwarding list so adding an experiment is a data change that cannot be forgotten; build-dir names include the new digits; the lane harness now prints `exp_on_compile_line=` from compile_commands.json and every lane body prints `KB E33 ENTER lane=N` so 'never called' is distinguishable from 'faulted inside'; and pre-relaunch verification at build time — EXP33=1 on the compile line, `kb_fwht_u2ld2` present in the ELF, `bench_fused` absent, which is positive proof the dispatch took the E33 branch. Durable rule, the compile-time twin of #333's symbol check: **assert the candidate's -D flag in compile_commands.json and its body symbol in the ELF before believing any number from an image** — a macro candidate produces no symbol and no link error, so a green build proves nothing at all.

asi.candidate: None — a harness iteration. Two full three-board batches (20260923T0715L, 20260923T0725L) and one partial (0740L) were spent before this was found: the flashed image contained bench_e32/bench_fused and no E33 code at all, while build_rc=0, flash_rc=0, the device booted, ran a complete bench and printed EVT KBENCH_DONE.
asi.root_cause: esp32/main/CMakeLists.txt forwarded ND_KB_EXP30/31/32 to the compiler but not ND_KB_EXP33, because each experiment's two lines had been hand-copied. '-DND_KB_EXP33=1' therefore sat unused in the CMake cache, the macro compiled as 0, and the dispatch silently fell through to the previous default body (bench_fused).
asi.why_every_check_missed_it: build_rc=0 (an uncompiled static function that is never called cannot fail to link); flash_rc=0; the board booted and completed; lane_macro_on_compile_line=4 (the LANE macro really was on the compile line); and the ELF symbol check grepped ${SYM:-bench_fused}... which I had parameterised to bench_e33, and it printed 0 — but the label still said bench_fused_in_elf, so the informative zero looked like the #347 nm-path false alarm. The only field that would have caught it was 'which experiment macro reached the compiler', which did not exist.
asi.second_hole: lane.sh named the build dir from EXP30/31/32 only, so an EXP33 build reused the all-zero directory name build-e29-000-1 — the same stale-CMakeCache trap the ledger already records twice ('fresh-configure every board: a stale board1 build dir dropped the asm kernel and read 4.2217'). The dir name now includes EXP33/EXP34.
asi.third_finding: a real memory-corruption bug in the E33 wide-load variant, found by reading the asm rather than by running it: kb_fwht_u2ld2 passed the same C pointer variable as both the load cursor (_a) and the store cursor (_c). ee.ldf.64.ip POST-updates its base register, so the two loads advance it 16 bytes and the two stores then write 16 bytes past the butterflies they read. The single-pair variant is correct only because it happens to use distinct variables. Fixed with separate sa/sb cursors and a comment at the site. It would have produced silently wrong rows (or a fault) in exactly the two lanes that use it.
asi.fixes: 1) CMakeLists: one foreach over 30..36 forwarding every ND_KB_EXPnn, so adding an experiment is a data change and cannot be forgotten (CMake comments must be '#' - my C-style block comment was itself a configure error, caught by the verification build). 2) lane.sh: build dir includes the new experiment digits, and it now prints 'exp_on_compile_line=' listing every DND_KB_EXPnn=1 found in compile_commands.json. 3) Each lane body prints 'KB E33 ENTER lane=N' first, so 'never called' is distinguishable from 'faulted inside'. 4) Pre-relaunch verification done at build time, not at harvest: EXP33=1 on the compile line, kb_fwht_u2ld2 present in needle_demo.elf, bench_fused absent (= the dispatch really took the E33 branch).
asi.generalisation: This is the compile-time-macro twin of run #333's 'an unreferenced new file is garbage-collected and the run silently re-measures the accepted runtime - nm the ELF for the candidate symbol'. For a macro candidate there is no symbol and no link error, so the rule has to be stronger: **assert the candidate's -D flag in compile_commands.json and its body symbol in the ELF before believing any number from the image.** That field is now printed by the lane harness itself.

description: Experiment 33 LANE 1 (board 1, kbench, EXP33 verified in the image; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward, no shipping change yet): the FWHT re-screened against the **shipped** `nd_fwht` rather than my reconstruction, and both the win and a trap came out of it. Shipped `nd_fwht` = 47,462 cycles for 2,688 butterflies (17.657 cyc/butterfly); C unroll-2 = **+17.95 % bit-exact**; the wide-load form (`ee.ldf.64.ip`/`ee.stf.64.ip` around the *same* scalar `add.s`/`sub.s`) = 34,706 cycles = **+36.75 % with diff=0 of 768 cells, bit-exact**; a 4-butterfly block form read **+87.30 %** and is **NOT bit-exact (diff=767)** because its loop condition `j+3 < i+len` never fires for `len==2`, so an entire stage is skipped — third "fast because it is wrong" caught by a differential in this campaign (#230's reorder, #335's lost nibble identity, this one a missing stage tail). Because the shipped transform is 47,462 of the engine's 58,902-cycle prepare, its share is **80.6 %**, not the 64.1 % my reconstruction implied — and with lane 2's rescale (18.3 %) and run #351's copy (3.3 %) the whole call is now attributed from the engine's own numbers. Recomputed prize: +36.75 % of 3.17 ms/token = 0.85 ms = **+0.43 % decode** on the transform alone, above the keep bar by itself. Integrated now (three boards: both / transform-only / rescale-only), gated on power-of-two n and 8-byte alignment with the generic loop as the fallback and the `len==1` stage left scalar because its `b` operand lives inside the same float pair as its `a`.

asi.candidate: LANE 1 (board 1, kbench): three variants of the FWHT butterfly loop, each diffed cell-by-cell against the SHIPPED nd_fwht symbol (not a transcription - run #338's rule), on the real geometry (6 groups x g=128 = 2,688 butterflies per round), min of 25 rounds.
asi.hypothesis: run #352 screened variants against MY reconstruction, which run #357 proved is not the engine's transform (762/768 cells differ). Re-screen against the shipped function so the delta is against what actually ships.
asi.result: shipped nd_fwht 47,462 cycles (17.657 cyc/butterfly); C unroll-2 40,238 (14.969) = +17.95 % bit-exact; wide-load pair form (ee.ldf.64.ip/ee.stf.64.ip around the same scalar add.s/sub.s) 34,706 (12.911) = **+36.75 % bit-exact (diff=0)**; 4-butterfly block 25,340 = +87.30 % but **diff=767 NOT_EXACT**.
asi.not_exact_catch: The +87.3 % block form has no small-stage tail: its loop condition is `j + 3 < i + len`, so for len==2 the body never runs and the whole stage is skipped - every downstream cell is then wrong. It is the third 'fast because it is wrong' this campaign has caught with a differential (#230's reorder, #335's wide-load nibble loss, this). Had it been bit-exact it would have been the largest kernel win of the campaign; it is instead the reason the shipped patch uses the pair form.
asi.accounting_bonus: The shipped FWHT costs 47,462 of the engine's 58,902-cycle prepare call = **80.6 %**, not the 64.1 % my reconstruction implied; with lane 2's rescale (10,789 = 18.3 %) and run #351's copy (1,954 = 3.3 %) the three sum to 60,205 vs 58,902 measured - so prepare is now fully attributed with the ENGINE's own numbers.
asi.prize_recomputed: transform = 80.6 % of a 0.2454 ms call x ~16 calls/token = 3.17 ms/token. +36.75 % on it = 0.85 ms/token = **+0.43 % decode**, on its own above the keep bar. The block form's fake +87 % would have printed +0.60 %, which is why the differential is the gate.
asi.next: integrated on three boards at 20260923T1015L: board 1 both changes, board 2 transform-only, board 3 rescale-only (an ablation batch - the combined reading cannot say which half carries it, nor whether nd_fwht's 8-byte-alignment gate ever fires on the real scratch buffer).
asi.gate_note: The integrated nd_fwht fast path is gated on n being a power of two and the block being 8-byte aligned, with the len==1 stage left scalar (its b operand lives inside the same float pair as its a operand) and the generic loop retained as the fallback for anything else. Alignment failure falls back silently, which is exactly why the rescale-only ablation is on its own board: if the combined delta equals the rescale-only delta, the gate never fired and the transform half is worth zero in situ.

description: Experiment 33 LANE 2 (board 2, kbench, EXP33 verified in the image; decode_tps is the accepted 5.0300 carried forward): the per-group rescale in `fwht_rows`, measured at the engine's own geometry (scale = 1/sqrtf(g), g=128, 6 groups). Shipped scalar loop 10,789 cycles (14.048 cyc/element) → **unroll-4 2,968 cycles (3.865) = +263.51 %, bit-exact (scale_mismatch=0)**, while **unroll-8 is 28.44 % WORSE** (15,076) — the same LX7 register-file ceiling the ledger recorded for `kron_apply`, now measured on a second kernel. The rescale is **18.3 %** of the engine's 58,902-cycle prepare, which combined with lane 1's 80.6 % transform and run #351's 3.3 % copy finally attributes the whole call from the engine's own numbers. Saving 7,821 cycles/call over ~16 calls/token is 0.52 ms = **+0.26 % decode on this half alone**, so both halves clear the keep bar independently and the predicted combined win is **+0.70 %** — the largest since the phi asm. Host side agrees: 16/16 repo tests, host_output_exact=19, token_delta 0, golden_missing 0, fidelity 5.341e-05 unchanged, top1 10/10. Disclosed: the rescale-only ablation file keeps the transform helper's (unused) definition, so it builds with a 'defined but not used' warning while behaving as a pure rescale-only image.

asi.candidate: LANE 2 (board 2, kbench): the per-group rescale that fwht_rows runs after the transform, at the engine's own geometry (scale = 1/sqrtf(g), g=128, 6 groups = 768 elements per call), diffed bit-for-bit. Variants: shipped scalar loop, unroll-4, unroll-8.
asi.hypothesis: the rescale was 14.5 % of my reconstructed prepare and run #352's isolated screen said unroll-4 halves it; measured against the shipped geometry it has an unknown share, and that share is what decides whether it is worth shipping at all.
asi.result: shipped 10,789 cycles (14.048 cyc/element); **unroll-4 2,968 (3.865) = +263.51 %, bit-exact (scale_mismatch=0)**; unroll-8 15,076 (19.630) = **-28.44 %, worse**. So the sweet spot is 4, exactly as the ledger's kron_apply finding predicts (reuse from the operand loaded per cell, and the LX7 register file stops paying past that).
asi.accounting: 10,789 of the engine's 58,902-cycle prepare = **18.3 %**, which closes the call's attribution with lane 1's 80.6 % transform and run #351's 3.3 % copy. Saving 7,821 cycles/call x ~16 calls/token = 0.52 ms/token = **+0.26 % decode** on this half alone - independently above the 0.2 % keep bar.
asi.verdict: KEEP as a candidate component. Combined with lane 1's bit-exact transform half (+0.43 %) the predicted total is **+0.70 %**, the largest single predicted win since the phi asm (#333, +0.365 %). Integration is measuring on three boards now; both halves are bit-exact by construction (an elementwise multiply has no accumulation order; the transform keeps the same scalar add/sub per cell) and the host agrees: 16/16 repo tests, host_output_exact=19, host_token_delta=0, host_golden_missing=0, fidelity 5.341e-05 unchanged, top1 10/10.
asi.next: harvest 20260923T1015L. If the combined candidate beats the bar and is byte-exact on device, keep both halves; the two ablation boards say whether the transform half is actually firing (its gate needs an 8-byte-aligned scratch block) or whether all of the delivered delta belongs to the rescale.
asi.disclosure: the rescale-only variant file still contains the transform helper's definition but not its use, so it compiles with a 'defined but not used' warning and behaves as pure rescale-only. Functionally correct, cosmetically noisy; noted so the warning is not mistaken for a real transform half.
