description: Wrote and ran the host-side bit-exactness guard for the seed win (.auto/exp87/test_seed_equiv.c), and it corrected my own claim before it could become a load-bearing citation. The seed replaces four per-group mov.s resets with the first four adds reading add.s f0, f6, fN where f6 is +0.0, and I had recorded that as 'arithmetically unchanged'. The test sweeps 4,182,161 fp32 values (every special, every value with <=4 significant bits across all exponents, plus a dense stride over the whole pattern space) and compares the add form against a move: the differences are exactly two classes, -0.0 (sign of zero) and every SIGNALING NaN (an addition quiets its operand, so 0xffbffe12 becomes 0xfffffe12) - 3 negative zeros and 8,137 sNaNs, zero unexplained. My first version asserted only the -0.0 class and failed on its own sweep, printing the sNaN case; that is the campaign's recurring lesson that a guard is what finds the hole in the argument, not a way to confirm it. Both classes are unreachable for the operand the seed sees (a pair-LUT entry is a product of finite codebook and activation values, so finite, +0.0, or a QUIET NaN - hardware arithmetic never emits an sNaN - and a -0.0 partial needs every term -0.0), and the independent empirical half is 6/6 primary plus 18/20 full-suite byte-exact on two boards. The exit code requires the difference set to equal exactly {-0.0, sNaN} and both classes present, so it cannot pass vacuously. No board time. Pin unchanged at 5.3033.

asi.durable_rule: An add from +0.0 is NOT bit-identical to a move: it differs for -0.0 (sign of zero) and for every signaling NaN (addition quiets it, ffbffe12 -> fffffe12). Any future 'seed from a zero register instead of resetting' change must clear those two classes, not just 'is it IEEE'.
asi.hypothesis: Give the confirmed seed win the bit-exactness proof the host gate cannot provide: characterise, over the fp32 space, exactly when add.s f0, +0.0, x differs from a reset-and-move.
asi.how_it_worked: First version of the test asserted the only exception was -0.0 and FAILED on its own sweep: 8,140 differences, and the printed one was x=ffbffe12, a signaling NaN, which the addition quiets to fffffe12. So the transformation has TWO exception classes, not one, and I found that by running the test rather than by reasoning about IEEE-754 - the same pattern as every other guard in this repo that caught my own assumption.
asi.reachability: The seed's first-add operand is a pair-LUT entry: a product of finite codebook and activation values, so it is finite, +0.0, or a QUIET NaN - hardware arithmetic never emits a signaling NaN. A -0.0 partial would need every term of that partial to be -0.0. Neither class can occur, and the empirical half is independent: 6/6 primary and 18/20 full-suite byte-exact on two boards with this kernel.
asi.why_host_matters: The host cannot compile the asm path at all, so for every kept assembly change in this campaign the only automatic veto is the device compare. A C-level characterisation of the transformation is the only host-side evidence that can exist, and now it does.
asi.test_exit: cc -O2 -ffp-contract=off .auto/exp87/test_seed_equiv.c -lm; exit 0 requires the difference set to equal exactly {-0.0, sNaN} AND both classes to be present as positive controls, so the guard cannot pass vacuously.
asi.next: Seed stack remains fully evidenced and owner-gated. No board used for this.

description: Wired the seed-win bit-exactness guard into .auto/checks.sh so it runs on every lane: build .auto/exp87/test_seed_equiv.c with cc -O2 -ffp-contract=off into the log directory and fail the checks on a non-zero result, plus an explicit C_GUARD_NO_COMPILER failure when the compiler is missing (a guard that passes because its tool is absent is this campaign's most-repeated self-inflicted bug). Verified end to end rather than by reading the diff: bash -n clean and a full checks.sh run came back green with the new stage in place, reporting host_lines_same=19 and FIDELITY steps=10 vocab=8192 max_delta=5.341e-05 top1=10/10, so the guard passed inside the real pipeline. This is the only host-side evidence that exists for an assembly change, because the host build compiles the C fallback - so the practical effect is that a future seeding edit whose difference set grows beyond {-0.0, signaling NaN} stops at the host stage instead of twelve minutes later on a board. .auto/exp41/test_cond_equiv.c deliberately stays manual since its build flags differ and guessing them into a mandatory path is the #359 failure mode. No board time. Pin unchanged at 5.3033 with the seed stack fully evidenced and owner-gated.

The compiler-missing branch is deliberate: a guard whose tool is absent must report failure, not pass - this campaign has found four of its own checks doing exactly that (#296 missing-golden-as-exact, the partial-save guard, the config check, and #530's /health token).

description: Recipe A unblocked without inline asm and launched. The fused branch therefore reproduces the shipped mul.s-then-two-madd.s rounding graph (rescale rounds on its own cell, each P.V update is one fused rounding) with no register barrier and no target-specific code, and because there is no asm the host build compiles the same expression, so the host golden is real evidence about the arithmetic. checks.sh rc=0 on the patched tree with host_lines_same=19 byte-exact, max_delta 5.341e-05, top1 10/10; board 2 is now screening it at provenance 9e658137ba25 against that board's own 5.6117 seed reading. Pin unchanged at 5.3033.

asi.hypothesis: Express recipe A's arithmetic without any inline asm: make the rescale a standalone multiply and the two P.V terms EXPLICIT __builtin_fmaf, so GCC cannot fold the multiply into a following add and the fused branch reproduces the shipped mul.s-then-two-madd.s graph.
asi.why_it_works: Contraction can only merge a standalone multiply into an adjacent add; it cannot fold a multiply into an explicit fma argument, so writing the P.V terms as fma makes the rescale round on its own cell exactly as the shipped separate pass did, and the two P.V updates stay single-rounding fused operations like the baseline madd.s pair. No register barrier, no target-specific asm, and the same C compiles on both sides so the host golden exercises the identical expression.
asi.mentor_correction_accepted: The 'implicitly popped registers' and 'output constraint 0 must specify a single register' errors were HOST gcc (x87, /usr/bin/cc per host/build/CMakeCache.txt), not Xtensa - so run #610 did not establish a Xtensa blocker and I mis-attributed it. Correct disposition: the guard belongs on the target path (volatile-temporary host fallback, +f on ESP_PLATFORM); I took the simpler route of no asm at all, which also lets the host gate actually test the expression instead of a fallback.

Price (boot-time microbenchmark, diagnostic only): the GCC-compiled C DOT8W body costs 49 cycles per 4-float chunk, the hand-written wide kernel 80 cycles/chunk (+63%), and the call boundary only 29 cycles per head-pair call. So the E51 microbenchmark's 38% never existed against the real baseline: E51 compared hand-written lsi with hand-written wide, both carrying the same fixed statement order, while GCC hoists loads and interleaves the four accumulator chains. End-to-end on b3: 5.4983 vs its own 5.6033 widephi pin = -1.87%, matching b2's -2.1% (uniform across decode/prefill/boot). Wide-load P.V kernel CONFIRMED cross-board and cross-base (E53 on b2, seed-era 5.8400 pin): decode 5.8767 = +0.63% - the identical delta the shippable line showed on b1 (5.5833 -> 5.6183), on a different base, a different quant/asm stack and a different board. Wide-load kron2 factor rows (E54, b1 shippable+notif+PV base) DISCARDED at -0.30%: decode 5.6017 vs the same board's PV-only 5.6183, boot 5.697 vs 5.712. The kernel is bit-exact (device selftest 64/64, pool_align=0, kron2=1 so it really ran) and the mechanism is a register-file limit, not a load-form failure: the shipped kron2 body keeps EIGHT live accumulators and re-reads 16 factor floats per j step, which is exactly why it can spend registers on accumulators. Four wide loads want four registers per row, so the kernel must either keep four accumulators and walk j twice (what this candidate did: double the loop overhead, double the crow reads, halve the ILP) or reload - and both cost more than the 12 lsi it removes. Rule reinforced: a wide-load substitution needs both removable redundant traffic AND enough free registers to hold the row; eight accumulators plus two factor rows do not fit in f0-f15.

Rule: guard cost is paid per call, so a kernel behind a rare branch needs the branch hoisted to the caller or the candidate is dead on arrival.

Wide delivery for the mHC lane mix (E64 on B2) - the campaign's biggest single lever since P.V, and the first one found in a phase that was never asked to be widened. The shipped body is five read-modify-write passes per output lane over d_model floats (init dst[i] = hpost[k]*u[i], then four passes of dst[i] += w*src[i] over the four input lane rows): contiguous rows, one madd per cell, no accumulator chain, and the compiler cannot keep dst in registers across the passes. Two kernels - nd_mul4w for the initialiser and nd_lanemix4w for each accumulation pass - move four cells per 128-bit load/store pair with the same single madd per cell and the same pass order, so the values are bit-identical (device selftest 64/64). Frozen-pair per-step diagnostic on B1: the probe is INVALID and produces no model-vs-sampler signal. `nd_sample_hidden(&s_model, &smp, lg)` hands back a logits pointer that is the constrained sampler's FILTERED subset, not the full-vocab array, so an argmax over the first `s_model.vocab` entries reads past it: every step of every case, including the passing control, reports the same bogus top1=989 with value 1.9e37 and chosenval near zero. The harness lesson is the campaign's oldest one in a new place - a probe must be validated against a case whose answer is known before its output is interpreted, and the control case did exactly that here. What IS valid from the harvest: the per-step chosen token ids are real (the sampler's own decisions), the three cases' texts reproduce the known behaviour (heldout_interval_one answers seconds=300 where the golden says 1; heldout_long_tools_note_only degenerates into a repeating "heap high water mark -> seconds 300" chain; the sampling5 control is correct), and the two failing cases share their first three chosen ids (6, 38, 8121) with the control before diverging - so the input path is identical up to the prompt, which matches the earlier qlen/qhash/token-id record. Next attempt at this diagnostic must read the sampler's own candidate list or the existing logits4 hook rather than indexing the subset pointer.

Frozen-pair diagnostic, second attempt and VALID this time: the probe now reads the constrained sampler's own legal candidate set and scores (nd_sample.c, behind ND_REQ_DIAG) instead of indexing the subset pointer, and prints the choice, how many tokens the grammar left legal, and the margin to the runner-up among them. Findings: (1) the choices are NOT razor-thin - the median margin over the runner-up legal token is ~12.8 logits (a probability ratio near 3.6e5) on both the failing case and the passing control, and the wrong picks are confident ones (the failing case picks seconds=300 with margin ~16); (2) the failing case and the passing control emit the SAME first six chosen tokens (507, 379, 300, 722, 8122, 8100) and separate only at the decision point, where the control concludes a single set_timer call and the long-tools case degenerates into a repeating "heap high water mark -> seconds 300" chain for 55 steps; (3) the grammar's legal set is small (3-14 tokens per step) so the sampler is choosing from a handful, but with wide margins. Together with the earlier input record (qlen/qhash/prefix identity all intact) this points at the model's own arithmetic/state on the longer prompt rather than at sampler tie-breaking - the shape to test next is the device's int8 KV cache accumulating more error over the longer prompt. One metric bug to note for reuse: margin=0 at legal=1 steps is not a razor-thin decision, and the script's razor_thin counter counted those.

Frozen-pair repeatability probe (B1, same diag image, both failing cases run twice in one process): every chosen token id and the full generated text are IDENTICAL between the two runs of each case - interval_one is 18 steps ending in the wrong `seconds=300` both times, long_tools is 55 steps of the same repeating chain both times, `first_diff_step=None` for both. So the wrong answers are deterministic arithmetic/state outcomes, not per-run nondeterminism. Combined with the previous window's evidence (inputs identical: qlen/qhash/encoded suffix ids/restored prefix identity; sampler choices confident with median margin ~12.8 logits; the failing case and the passing control share their first six chosen ids), the picture is now bounded on three sides: the divergence is downstream of the prompt, upstream of the sampler's tie-breaking, and reproducible within an image. That also bounds #647: since one image is deterministic here, the ring's flip must be a PERSISTENT state difference the ring establishes before or at the request (what got primed/restored), not per-step timing jitter. The remaining decisive step is a device-vs-host per-step logits comparison on these two cases, which needs the host logits captured at the same steps rather than another device-only probe.

Attention-input in-place prepare (E72 on B1) DISCARDED at -6.3%: the same lifetime shape that paid three times (nx/xh, dequant row, and the MLP conditioning) LOSES here. The change redirected the attention's input RMS to emit into xh and passed xh to attention() - whose only use of its input is the projection prepare, which already skips a self-copy - so a 768-float copy per layer should have disappeared with identical arithmetic. Device output is 6/6 byte-exact, so the arithmetic is right, yet decode reads 5.4100 against this board's 5.7767 base while the boot bench is UNCHANGED (5.894 vs 5.877). That split is the interesting part: the short-context boot bench does not see it, the primed-prefix decode does, which is not what a copy removal should look like - the likely mechanism is cache/buffer interaction (xh is the same buffer the FWHT/LUT prepare and the mHC phi path transform in place, so the attention's transform now runs on a buffer that has just been written by a different producer, and the prefix path touches that pattern far more often than the 6-token cold bench). Recorded as an unexplained but unambiguous regression; B1 was restored byte-exactly to 78c435fec440 and rebuilds. Anyone re-attempting in-place attention should measure the PREFIX path specifically and instrument cache behaviour, not just the boot bench.

Elementwise-product family (E73 on B1) FAILED HARD: device_output_exact 0/6 and decode 3.125, boot bench 4.441 - a correctness failure, not a slow result. The candidate widened four shapes at once: dst = a*b for the conditioned input (new nd_mul2w kernel), dst += scalar*src for the engram injection and the attention residual (existing nd_lanemix4w), and dst += a*b for the MLP residual fold (new nd_mac2w kernel). The campaign's own rule is that every new kernel gets its own differential oracle before it is trusted - the four mix-family kernels each have one - and these two new kernels were wired in with none, so a 0/6 device gate is exactly what a missing oracle looks like. The most likely single defect is in one of the two new kernels rather than in the two reuse sites (whose shapes are already proven). Recorded as the failure mode, not as a closed family: the four shapes are legitimately widenable (each is one mul or one madd per cell over contiguous rows), and the correct next attempt is one shape at a time, each with an oracle of the form the mix family uses. B1 was restored byte-exactly to 78c435fec440 and rebuilds. Cost: one board run plus the analysis; no gate was weakened and nothing was kept.

Device-vs-host comparison for the frozen pair, using the host generator that does exist (nd_dump genp, nothink, exactly as bench.py invokes it) - and it reframes the two failures as MODEL behaviour rather than engine defects. Host results: `Sample telemetry every second` -> a single set_sampling_interval seconds=120 in 23 tokens; `Sample telemetry every 5 seconds` -> set_sampling_interval seconds=5 in 22 tokens; the long multi-tool prompt -> set_sampling_interval 45 then set_timer 300 THREE TIMES then get_status, 67 tokens. That repetition is the same tendency the device shows, so the device's long-tools answer is not a device arithmetic defect - the host, running the same engine and archive, repeats the same call. Two further facts fall out: the host's interval_one answer (120 alone) matches what the device produced in the frozen think=0 mode, and the host's CONTROL answer picks a different tool (set_sampling_interval) than the device does (set_timer) for the same phrasing - while the device passes that case against its golden. So the goldens are device-derived artefacts of a particular run state, not host-derived truth, and the two failures sit on prompts where the model itself is unstable between two plausible answers. This is the owner-decision evidence the two-case blocker has been missing: it is not an arithmetic bug to find, it is a stability/re-baseline question. NOTE for the ledger: earlier 'device degenerates on long_tools' readings came from think=1 harvests; the frozen mode is think=0 and must be used for any further comparison.

Frozen-pair STATE sensitivity test (B1, frozen think=0 mode, same image): both failing cases were run FIRST (immediately after priming) and LAST (after three other requests had run) and produce byte-identical answers in both positions - interval_one `set_sampling_interval seconds=120` and the long-tools case the same 45-then-timer chain - so the answers are stable under request ordering and accumulated state. Together with the repeatability result (identical across repeated runs) the device is fully deterministic AND order-independent on this image, which removes within-image state accumulation from the mechanism list. Since every lever landed in these images is bit-exact on the other 18 cases, and the host (same engine, fresh prefill) now produces the SAME interval_one answer the device does, the remaining explanation is the one #647 already isolated: the accept/reject difference is tied to what the RING carries into the request path (it flips exactly this pair when added to an otherwise unchanged engine), i.e. it is a re-baseline decision - keep the ring and re-baseline/replace these two cases, or drop the ring and lose the >128-byte request fix and the 20-case suite. That is an owner choice, not something a further probe or engine change can resolve without one of those two acts.

Dead code is not free, and it invalidated two of this window's results. B1's tree with the inert DIAGPICK/DIAGREQ hook (78c435fec440, every added line behind #ifdef, plus a stdio include in nd_sample.c) reads 5.4100 with boot 5.893, against 5.7767 with boot 5.877 for the same stack without the hook (bae5184f9ca7) - a 6.3% decode regression from scaffolding that compiles to nothing, with the boot bench unmoved. A contemporaneous control on the other board (B2, untouched tree, allowed repeat with a recorded reason) still reads 6.0450 / boot 6.155 / 18-of-20, so the boards and the environment did not drift and the loss is real and reproducible. Consequences: (1) E72's -6.3% and E74's -6.4% were measured against the WRONG baseline - both are neutral, and E72's buffer-interaction story is retracted; (2) any lane that measures a candidate on a tree carrying diagnostic scaffolding gets a wrong baseline, so scaffolding must be stripped (or the tree's own baseline measured) before a candidate is priced; (3) the split itself is a clue - the short cold boot bench is blind to it while the primed-prefix decode is not, which is the same split E72 showed us and I mis-attributed. The mechanism is almost certainly sampler-path codegen: nd_sample.c is walked once per token and its inlining decisions move with an added include, so a hook there is not inert in the compiled image.

Dominant-path closure, derived from the source rather than from memory. The live 2-bit walker's hot body is the W8D macro, whose per-word accounting is exactly 8 lsi (LUT lookups) + 8 extui (index extraction) + 8 addx4 (address formation) + 8 add.s (accumulation) = 32 instructions, plus one 32-bit word load per word - 33 instructions for 16 weights, i.e. 2.06 per weight. Every one of them is irreducible on this ISA: the pair table is the largest granularity that still fits a cache line (the quad-table variant measured 38% slower), each lookup needs its own extract + scaled-index form + load because the ISA has no base+scaled-index load, 16 weights need 8 lookups because each table entry folds two codebook products, and 8 adds are the accumulation itself. The field cost is ~16.4 cycles per word, i.e. ~2 instructions per cycle, which is dual-issue saturation - so the phase that is 59% of the token (proj2bit, 80.8 ms) sits at the ISA floor with the measured IPC pinned against its instruction budget. This is why every load-form, scheduling, register and layout attempt in that phase has come back neutral or negative: there is no instruction to remove. The same argument covers the engram's GEMVs (same walker; I also verified in the same pass that nd_cq_gemv_lut2 already splits across both cores, so there is no idle-core lever hidden there either). Hardware: all three consoles silent on one bounded probe each, no loops, nothing reflashed; both packets stand unchanged.

Two results in one window. (1) LSX IS IMPLEMENTED on this silicon - #732's capability closure is RETRACTED. The first probe passed indices 0,1,2 to `lsx`, but LSX takes a BYTE offset (Espressif's own FIR kernels multiply by 4 first), so 1 and 2 were misaligned addresses. The corrected probe with byte offsets 0,4,8,60,64 on an aligned table prints `LSX2 mask=1f vals=11.000,22.000,33.000,55.000,66.000` - all five offsets load the right float, including one past a cache line - so the uint16 offset-stream mechanism (l16ui -> lsx -> add.s instead of extui -> addx4 -> lsi -> add.s) is CAPABLE here and its remaining question is cost, not existence. (2) The four-accumulator register-resident scale fold (nd_scrow4 on B1) is bit-exact and live - SCROW selftest 64/64 bad=0, scrow=1, 6/6 device exact - and it LOSES at -0.09% (5.8233 vs the 5.8283 base). Two self-inflicted bugs were caught by the selftest before any number was believed: `movi a7,1; wfr f0,a7` loads the float bits 0x00000001 (a denormal), not 1.0f, and the row pointer never rewound per tile so tile 2 started eight strides in; the first run's oracle therefore read bad=1024 and its speed was the fallback. With both fixed the oracle is clean and the kernel is still slightly negative: keeping four cells resident replaces independent whole-row passes (E72b's, which the parallel split can overlap) with one serial eight-madd chain per tile, so the removed loads do not pay for the exposed latency. Banked as a negative; B1's tree restored to the 5.8283 state.

CV3W cost measured on device, and it is a real lever: with an identical work loop (eight lookups plus eight adds per 32-bit weight word, four partials, two adds each - the shipped W8D structure) and only the addressing changed, the shipped form (extui + addx4 + lsi) costs 34 cycles per word and the proposed form (l16ui of a predecoded uint16 byte offset + lsx) costs 25, i.e. 27% cheaper on the addressing itself, with the LSX capability probe still green (mask=1f). Fixture integrity is asserted: 64 words of 8 distinct 4-bit indices, a 16-entry float LUT, and the predecoded offsets checked against the nibbles (fixture_bad=0), so a fast wrong mapping cannot masquerade as a win. Both loops fold their partials into a sink that is mixed into the returned cycle count. This turns the LSX reopen from a capability question into a measured cost win, and it makes the capacity question the gating one: the offset stream is 4x the packed indices (442,368 B for a 576x768 Q projection) while post-prime PSRAM is only 50,088 B - which is exactly what B3's engram relocation into the tier buffer's unused tail is for (~791 KB reclaimable). Two-step program, both halves measured or specified: free the tier tail (B3), then integrate the offset stream (B2, one projection at a time, exact mapping/row/group checks).

B3's engram relocation ran and was correctly REFUSED by its own disjointness guard - a guarded null that answers a capacity question with numbers. Print: `EGRELOC ok=0 need=8997952 span=12582912 staged_rel=12450880`. Reading: the value slot's end needs 8,997,952 bytes and the span is 12,582,912 (both match the plan exactly), but the highest byte any CONTAINED tensor stages is 12,450,880 relative to eg_region_lo - higher than the specified key slot 8,684,608 and higher than the "last actual tier consumer" figure the plan was built on. The guard compares against tensor CONTAINMENT, which is the safe criterion: a contained tensor's bytes are physically copied into the span, so overlapping them would corrupt whatever does read them. Two consequences, both measured: (1) the span's genuinely unused tail is 12,582,912 - 12,450,880 = 132,032 bytes, which is smaller than the 313,344-byte key/value pair, so this route cannot host the relocation as specified; (2) the CV3W offset stream's capacity must therefore come from the reserve - compact-prefix, which reclaims ~791 KB (the mentor's fallback) - not from the tier tail. Decode 6.0550 with the dispatch off is the base (the candidate did nothing). Nothing was flashed twice, no gate was weakened, and the code is kept in B3's tree behind its guard so a corrected slot derivation is a one-line change if a future window establishes the true consumer set.

Compact saved prefixes: the capacity enabler for the CV3W offset stream is IN PLACE and measured. prefix_copy used to save the whole 384-slot KV window for each of the two prefixes even though the prefixes are 143/213 slots; the four KV buffers now copy only the prefix's LIVE slots (a new strided prefix_kv helper; same layout, same order, same values for everything that is read - only the image is smaller), and the restore assigns the prefix's state BEFORE the copy so the live count is the prefix's own rather than the model's current position. Quality: the host prefix-isolation test PASSES ("alternating prefixes reproduce identical logits", rc=0), which is the strongest check for the schema-switch path this change touches. Device: decode 5.8283 = the base unchanged (expected - the restore sits outside the decode clock), 6/6 exact, and the direct capacity measurement through the status API reads free_psram_bytes 818,596 against the 50,088 baseline, i.e. 768,508 bytes reclaimed. That is more than the 442,368 B a 576x768 offset stream needs, so the measured 27%-cheaper addressing (34 -> 25 cycles/word, #745) now has room. The CV3W offset-stream screen faulted before its print (inline-asm register allocation in my own bench, not an engine result), so it produced no device data - and while restoring the tree I priced the plan on the campaign's OWN measured numbers, which close it: the dominant proj2bit phase reads 3.59 MB per token in 80.8 ms = 44 MB/s, i.e. 69% of the measured 64 MB/s octal bus peak, and the offset stream is 1 byte per weight = 4x the packed stream = 14.36 MB per token, which needs 224 ms even at an unattainable 100% bus utilisation - 2.8x SLOWER than the 80.8 ms it replaces. The addressing win it buys is 8 addx4 removed from 33 instructions per 32-bit word = 24% of the issue slots, worth at most 19.6 ms, so it cannot pay for a 143 ms byte increase. The isolated 34 -> 25 cycles/word result (#745) was measured on a 64-word fixture that lives in the 64 KB data cache, so its streaming cost never appeared - the same warm-screen artifact this campaign recorded twice (#295 phi, #364 transform). Consequence: the predecoded offset stream is closed on the byte budget, and the tier-tail capacity work (#746/#747) and the compact-prefix reclaim (#748, 768 KB, quality-safe) stand on their own as free PSRAM and a faster prefix restore rather than as enablers for it. B1's throwaway screen build was fully reverted and rebuilt.

Instruction-level peephole audit of the hottest code (the 2-bit walker, 49% of the token) on the campaign-best image - a closure with evidence rather than an estimate, at zero board cost. The live nd_lut2_rows_tie1n body from board 2's 6.0617 ELF contains exactly 316 instructions: add.s 67 (64 accumulate + 3 fold), extui 64, addx4 64, lsi 64, l32i.n 16, then the group bookkeeping (slli 4, add.n 4, addmi 4, addi.n 4, mull 2, wfr 2, j 3, mov.s 2, plus entry/bgeu/sub/beqz). Read as a sequence, the body is exactly the documented W8D floor - extui x4 / addx4 x4 / lsi x4, then add.s x8, repeating for the eight 32-bit words of a 128-weight group - with no redundant instruction, no spill, and no reload: the 16 l32i.n all sit in the PROLOGUE (argument-struct fields, the two slice loads, the group norm), i.e. per call rather than per group. Every one of the 64 addx4 is the nibble's x4 byte scaling, which the ISA requires for a base+immediate-only lsi; every lsi is a pair-LUT lookup; every add.s is the accumulation. So the walker is at its instruction floor by direct inspection, which is the same conclusion the campaign reached analytically (2 instructions per weight, IPC ~1.33) and now has instruction-level evidence for. No candidate came out of the audit and no code changed.

Second peephole pass, on the other shipped kernels of the campaign-best (6.0617) image, for the two failure modes the load-form program identified: register pressure (spills) and redundant loads. Results, all static bodies read from the live ELF: nd_gemv4_rows_tie1W (wide phi) 76 instructions, 2 wide loads, 0 stack references; nd_gemv4_rows_tie1 (plain phi) 85 instructions, 16 lsi, 0 stack refs; nd_kron1_w (the kept wide kron) 33 instructions with 8 wfr / 8 madd.s / 8 ssi - the deliberately wider form, still no frame traffic; fwht_rows 414 instructions (46 l32i.n, 39 ssi, 38 lsi), 0 stack refs; nd_fwht3s (the fused stage-pair transform) 230 instructions (36 lsi, 36 ssi, 20 addx4 for float-stride address arithmetic, 18 each add.s/sub.s/mul.s), 0 stack refs; lanepre_rows 67 instructions, 0 stack refs. So the spill class - the one that decided the kron2 versus kron1 outcomes - is verified ABSENT on every kernel the newest tree ships, by direct inspection rather than by inheritance from the older scan; and no kernel carries an obviously redundant memory operation in its body. No candidate emerged, no code changed. Consolidated kernel inventory for the next window: the hot path is attn_heads (6,486 B of C including its inlined kernels), nd_model_step_hidden (7,241 B), nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (918 B, audited last run at exactly the W8D floor), nd_gemv4_rows_tie1W, nd_kron1_w, fwht_rows and nd_fwht3s.

Instruction-level read of attn_heads (the 24.1 ms phase, never audited before) - explanatory rather than a candidate, and it reconciles three historical nulls. Parsed from the live 6.0617 ELF: 2,414 instructions, ZERO frame accesses (no spill), 33 backward branches forming the nested loops, and a striking composition - movi 252 + l32r 160 = 412 instructions (17%) are constant materialization. Mapped to loop spans, the share is the same inside the hot bodies: the outermost loop (2,255 instrs) carries 406 constants (18%), the 1,696-instruction loop 288 (17%), the 1,202-instruction loop 201 (17%), the 818-instruction loop 132 (16%). Since attn_heads has no frame traffic at all, those constants are not spill refills: GCC is choosing to REMATERIALIZE addresses and float constants rather than keep them live, which is exactly the trade it makes when the 16-entry float register file is the binding resource (the same pressure that decided kron2 versus kron1 in the load-form program). That is the explanation for a previously unexplained pattern in this ledger: the live-range/hoist family measured THREE nulls (#579 quartet barriers -0.090%, #582 pointer+codebook hoist -0.060%, E-live-range edits -0.06%) even though the constants are visibly there - forcing them live costs registers the loop does not have, so the instruction count does not move. It also bounds the two directions: hoisting is closed by those measurements, and reducing the constant COUNT (algebraic restructuring of the exp polynomial or the clamp bounds) would be a rounding change, which the byte-exact and fidelity gates refuse. So the attention phase's remaining instruction budget is register-limited rather than redundant, and no candidate came out of the audit. No code changed.

Porting the seed line's NF16V lever to the shippable line INVERTS its sign: +0.642% there, -1.11% here (decode 5.765 against this board's own 5.83 tree) - a clean, measured verdict on a mathematically exact transformation. What was ported: the five-instruction fp16-to-fp32 rebias in lut2_tie728.S ((h<<13) + 0x38000000, which is exact for a positive ordinary halfword because m<<13 cannot carry into the exponent field and e+112 stays clear of 255) plus the load-bearing predicate extension in nd_lut2_asm_ok (reject sign-bit-set or exponent 0/31 norms, because a negative halfword's sign would land in the exponent; the census says every needle3.cact norm passes - 351,744 across 46 CQ2 tensors are positive normal). The port was verified before any board time: the host oracle over all 65,536 encodings printed REBIAS in_domain=30720 rejected=34816 mismatch=0 guard_miss=0 known_bad=0 and h=0x3c00 -> 3F800000, and the macro was byte-identical to the seed line's after the edit. Device: 6/6 exact, token_delta 0, boot bench unchanged, so the values are right and this is purely a speed verdict. The lesson is the campaign's composition rule with a new and stronger example - a lever's SIGN, not just its magnitude, depends on the tree it lands in (sub-additivity was known from bundle5; inversion is new), so the +0.642% measured on the seed stack was never a property of the transformation. CORRECTION to run #760: the engram[1] (EG2) candidate was very likely never executed at all. BLOCKER, no measurement: board 1 is strap-wedged in ROM download mode and the EG2 retry cannot run on it. The FP32 norm-sidecar probe - the last outstanding discovery item - is CLOSED OFF-DEVICE by the byte budget, before any purpose-built bench was written. The idea was to store the 2-bit stream's per-group norms as fp32 so the kernel could drop the NF16V fp16-to-fp32 rebias and load the scale with a plain lsi (5 instructions down to 1 per group). Priced on the campaign's own measured numbers for the dominant phase: the 2-bit stream is 3.59 MB/token = 14.36 M weights = 112.2 k groups of 128, so the norms are 224 KB/token as fp16 and 449 KB as fp32 - an extra 224 KB, which is +6.25% of the packed stream; at the measured 44 MB/s that phase sustains (69% of a 64 MB/s peak) the extra bytes cost +5.1 ms/token, while the four instructions removed per group come to 0.45 M instructions = 1.4 ms/token at the measured 1.33 IPC and 240 MHz. NET = -3.7 ms/token, about -2.4% decode, so the steady state loses by more than twice what it wins. Neither escape hatch exists: the norms cannot be kept fp16 and pre-converted (fp16 is fp16), and 224 KB cannot be cached against a 64 KB data cache. This is the same lesson the CV3W offset stream taught in run #749 and it now has a second worked example on a completely different payload: price a change in BYTES per token before pricing it in cycles per word, because this part's octal bus is at ~69% utilisation on the dominant stream and any stream that grows by a few percent pays more than a handful of instructions can recover. Consequence for the queue: the FP32 norm-sidecar item is retired (it needs no bench and no board), which leaves the campaign with every tree fully gated (B3 6.1433 the best, B2 6.1250, B1 5.9033), all three sharing only the two frozen #647 heldout cases as an owner disposition, and no remaining above-bar candidate that is not either already measured or closed by budget, gate or vendor support. Nothing was kept, no board time spent, no file changed.

The prepared 36-byte group-record experiment is refuted off-device by line-granularity arithmetic, before the asm and the bench it would have needed were written - and the refutation is decisive rather than marginal. Today's layout costs 0.531 lines per group (34 B of bus traffic): the packed side is dense enough to put two groups in a 64-byte line, and the fp16 norms live in their own dense array that amortises THIRTY-TWO norms per line, so the "second stream" the record was meant to merge away was costing 1/32 of a line per group, not one line. A merged 36-byte record, with a uniform start offset, spans two lines 12.5% of the time because 36 does not divide 64, so it costs 1.125 lines per group = 72 B - 2.12x the traffic. The experiment's own stated counter-argument turned out to be the thing that kills it, which is exactly why the rule exists: price a change in BYTES at line granularity before writing the kernel. Fixed the product defect this campaign has been flagging since run #155 and never closed: esp32/main/main.c silently truncated a request line at 271 bytes and answered as if the request were complete. The reader stored ND_LINE_MAX-1 characters and counted the rest in rx_drop, but the counter was never reported and the truncated line still went to run_inference, so a host sending a long request got an answer to its first 271 characters with no error of any kind - the campaign's own write-up called it "a real product defect for any host that sends arbitrary user text". The fix is five lines in the reader: if rx_drop is non-zero the line is refused explicitly with ERR line_too_long plus the limit and the true length, and nothing further is inferred from it. VERIFIED ON DEVICE, not by inspection: with the new firmware flashed on B3, a raw 316-byte request (written with the verified serial discipline - constructor closed, DTR/RTS false before and after open, bypassing the client library which guards at 255 bytes itself) produced exactly `ERR line_too_long max=271 got=316` followed by END, and a normal request in the same session still returned a correct `set_timer seconds=45` call. NO METRIC IMPACT: the frozen prompts are all <= 89 bytes, so this path never fires in the benchmark, and the normal-path check above confirms the console still serves ordinary requests - the change is about what a host learns when it sends something too long, which is now the truth instead of a silently shortened answer. This is main.c, which the project's scope note says may be touched to fix a real bug, and no engine file was involved. One housekeeping consequence: B3's tree now carries this fix, so its PROV_ENGINE hash differs from the value recorded in the handoff (3194872920a7bf7b19d378a9313ca9b4 was before the fix); the recorded pin 6.1450 stands, since the fix is outside the engine and outside the timed path. The other open product note from the same list - the schema's lack of a no-op escape, which turns chit-chat into a hallucinated set_sampling_interval - is a schema/behaviour decision for the owner, not something the loop should change.

Audited the rest of the request path for the same defect class as the truncation I just fixed - SILENT failure, the class this campaign's own ledger calls its highest-yield question ("can this check fail, and can it pass for the right reason?") - and the audit closes the class with evidence rather than with a guess. Three places a silent failure could hide, and their state: (1) the ANSWER side is already reported: main.c prints ERR generation_truncated produced=<tokens> bytes=<n> reason=<...> when generation hits the limit, and the MAX_NEW comment records that the previous 128 limit "silently corrupted" valid long tool-call lists and was raised to 256 for exactly that reason - so the answer path tells the host when it was cut off. (2) The per-token text copy is guarded defensively (''if (w + strlen(pc) < sizeof(out) - 1)'') and is backed by that same explicit truncation report, so a full output buffer cannot pass unnoticed. (3) Model-step return values are used or deliberately discarded in ways that cannot fail silently: where the logits pointer matters it is assigned and consumed immediately by the sampler, and a NULL there would fault loudly in the sampler rather than produce a quiet wrong answer; the priming and bench sites discard it because they only advance state. So the request path now has exactly one truncation that used to be silent - the 271-byte request line, fixed in #821 and verified in #823 - and the class is otherwise already handled correctly by code that predates this session. Audited the harness protection this session leaned on most - the anti-repeat allowance - and found it is enforced rather than merely documented, which is a stronger result than the check was looking for. The code path in measure.sh: a shipping signature already present in the signature history makes the run refuse with UNCHANGED_SHIPPING_IMAGE_REFUSED and exit 42, so an unchanged control cannot be re-measured by accident; an explicit AUTO_ALLOW_REPEAT=1 is then required, and a run without AUTO_REPEAT_REASON exits 43; and crucially, a tree that has already spent its confirmation hits REPEAT_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED and exit 44, because the allowance is recorded per signature in a repeat-history file rather than trusted to the operator's memory. When the allowance is legitimately used the script prints EXPLICIT_REPEAT_ALLOWED with the signature and the reason, so every use is in the log. My hypothesis going in was the opposite - that the "one allowance per tree" rule was a human convention with nothing enforcing it - and it is wrong: the machinery implements exactly the rule the documentation claims, with three distinct exit codes for the three failure modes. That matters for everything this window produced, because the B1, B2 and B3 promotions I ran all used that allowance exactly once per tree, and the guard would have refused a second use had I attempted one. It also closes the harness-integrity audit cleanly: the anti-repeat budget is enforced, PROV_ENGINE covers engine/src/*.c, *.S, engine/include/*.h and esp32/main/*.c, EXPECT_ENGINE_MD5 refuses a mismatched tree before it starts, and the metric-line inconsistency I fixed in #826 was the one real crack in that wall. No engine code changed, no board time spent, nothing promoted. Pool unchanged: B3 6.1450, B2 6.1250, B1 5.9283; best gated packet 6.1433 = +15.8% over the accepted 5.3033.

Audited the last unexamined gate set, .auto/checks.sh (82 lines, the quality authority that runs after every passing benchmark), for the vacuous-pass class that produced four real holes earlier in this campaign - and it comes out clean. Every gate family is fail-safe by construction: the host build and the native tests and ctest each exit 1 with a named error; the frozen-input guard keys on git status; the bench-guards test and the seed-equivalence test both check for their compiler first and refuse with C_GUARD_NO_COMPILER if it is missing (the lesson from the earlier bug where a check keyed on IDF_PATH reported success while verifying nothing); the primary-prompt hash and the serial guard exit 1 on failure. The two patterns that matter most are both done correctly. First, tool presence is checked by command, not by an environment variable: 'command -v cmake' and 'command -v cc' with an explicit exit, which is exactly the rule the campaign learned the hard way. Second, and this is the subtle one, every metric compared is defaulted so that a MISSING reading fails rather than passes - '${exact:-0}' against '${cases:-1}' fails when the case count is absent, '${missing:-1}' treats an unparsed golden_missing as incomplete, and the fidelity check defaults delta to 999 so an unparsed value is rejected against the 2e-3 threshold. That is precisely the fix for the class of bug where a typo'd case id counted as byte-exact: the default now points at failure, never at success. So the whole harness audit is complete and positive: the anti-repeat budget is enforced with three distinct exit codes, PROV_ENGINE covers every engine source plus main.c, EXPECT_ENGINE_MD5 refuses a mismatched tree, checks.sh has eight fail-safe gate families with no vacuous passes, and the single real crack found this session - the metric-line hash inconsistency of #826 - is fixed. Closed the last item on the campaign's oldest open list - "iteration speed, not the metric" - by resource arithmetic rather than by building it. The item proposed halving the ~5 min per flash spent priming the two schema prefixes, either by priming them concurrently on the two cores or by caching a primed prefix in flash. Both routes are dead: the two prefixes are sequential phases of ONE model state (prefix 1 runs from a reset, then prefix 2 runs from a reset), so they are not independent work that can be handed to the second core; doing them in parallel would require two model instances, and a second instance costs about 13 MB of PSRAM against the ~517 KB free after open on this board - impossible on this part. Flash-caching a primed prefix would need its own partition, and partitions.csv is frozen by the project's off-limits list. Recorded in .auto/ideas.md and as a final closure note in the queue. Audited the one surface I had never verified - the primary metric's own definition - and it is honest, computed exactly as documented. In .auto/bench.py the outer loop walks the requested groups and a FRESH tps list is built per group, so the metric line is the mean over that group's cases alone rather than over everything measured; each per-case value is the DEVICE's own reported number (r['decode_tps'], i.e. the firmware's 'EVT done ... tps='), not a host-side recomputation; and the aggregate is round(mean(tps), 4). The primary group resolves to exactly the six documented prompts - sampling5, timer60, status_heap, batch, heldout_timer45, route_translate - which matches the campaign's own arithmetic check from earlier in the ledger, where the six per-case rates reproduced the aggregate to the digit. Two related properties came out of the same read and are worth recording: a case that never saw 'EVT done' has None metrics and the aggregates use 'or 0.0', so a wedged case drags the mean DOWN rather than being skipped - a failure can never flatter the number; and the diagnostic inter-case gap (AUTO_CASE_GAP_S, used for the wedge investigation) is metric-safe by construction for the same reason the device is the authority, since the firmware times its own decode window and an idle gap between requests cannot enter it. So the audit set is now complete and positive across every surface: the metric's definition and aggregation, the quality gates (checks.sh, eight fail-safe families), the anti-repeat budget (enforced, exits 42/43/44), provenance coverage, the whole request path's silent-failure class, the artifacts and assets against the live workers, and the documentation itself. Found and fixed the sixth instance this session of something silently meaning less than it claims - and this one was in my own recovery check. The gap: .auto/trees/verify.sh compared each snapshot only against the hash embedded in its FILENAME, so it printed SNAPSHOT_OK and TREE_SNAPSHOTS_OK while board 3's live tree had already moved on. That is exactly the failure the snapshots exist to prevent: a recovery artifact that no longer matches the tree it is supposed to recover, and the check I wrote to guard it could not see that case because it only ever tested internal consistency. I found it by asking what the check should do when a tree changes after its snapshot - board 3's qk_hd == 48 specialization from #844 landed after the snapshot, so its live hash (ad9804745c88) no longer matched the recorded 2b7d119bdc44, and running the verifier confirmed it said OK anyway. Closed the dominant phase by principle instead of by another null, which is the strongest form of closure this campaign can produce and the statement a future window actually needs. proj2bit is 79.7 ms, 49.7% of the token, so it is the one phase where a few percent would move the headline result; the accounting is now arithmetic rather than a list of ~20 measured nulls. Per 32-bit index word (16 weights) the kernel executes 8 add.s (the accumulation, one per two weights, and the four-partial split is what hides the rest of the latency), 8 extui (the ISA has no scaled-index load from a register, and byte loads give two nibbles that still need shift+and, so extraction can be moved but not removed), 8 addx4 (lsi takes base+immediate only, so the nibble's 4-byte scaling must be materialised), 8 lsi (the pair-table lookups) and one l32i for the word itself. That is 24 ALU ops = 12 cycles at the S3's 2-wide issue, against ~16 measured, the difference being load-use and dependency slack - which reproduces the campaign's measured IPC of 1.33 exactly (32 instructions / 16 cycles / 2 wide). So the phase is issue-bound at a budget every instruction of which is forced by the addressing model of this ISA, and the only escape - a predecoded offset stream that removes the scaling - costs 4x the bytes and was already measured dead against a bus at 69% utilisation (#749: 14.36 MB/token, 2.8x slower even at an unattainable 100% bus). Consequence, now recorded in the backlog: no scheduling, unrolling, register, layout or load-width idea can move this phase, and that is a statement about the instruction set rather than about the nulls; the only lever left would change what is stored, which the byte-exact and fidelity gates refuse. No engine code changed, no board time spent, no metric moved; pins stand at B3 6.1450 / B2 6.1250 / B1 5.9283 with the best gated packet at 6.1433 = +15.8% over the accepted 5.3033.

Searched for a real lever in the next-largest phase and found, in the compiled code, that it is already taken - which is a useful closure rather than an empty iteration. The hypothesis: attention and the MLP are full of a*b + c patterns, the S3's FPU has madd.s (a fused multiply-add), so those pairs could be one instruction instead of two - a large instruction-count win that the byte-exact gate would ordinarily forbid because fusion changes the rounding. The first step was to check whether contraction is actually off, and it is NOT: attn_heads in the linked image contains 119 madd.s against 58 mul.s and 29 add.s, so GCC has already fused every pairable multiply-add, and the engine's component CMakeLists carries no -ffp-contract=off (that flag exists only in the campaign's test builds, where it is needed to make bit comparisons meaningful). The residual multiplies and adds are standalone operations, not halves of a pair. So the FP instruction budget of the attention path is already at its floor and no "enable FMA" proposal should ever be made here again - it was never disabled. This is the third item this session found already shipped rather than missing, after the int8 K/V word reads (#816) and the answer-side truncation report (#825), and it is why "prove the code is absent before pricing it" is now the first step of any candidate review in this campaign: the linked image is the authority, and one opcode scan settles in seconds what a design discussion cannot. Verified the ledger's claim about the third-largest phase against the linked image instead of trusting the summary, and the claim holds. kron_apply's two kernels, counted from the ELF: kron1_blocks contains 8 madd.s for 8 products (the eight-accumulator pass) alongside 6 lsi, 8 ssi, 6 addx4, 7 add.n, 6 mov.n, 3 loop and 3 extui; kron2_rows contains 17 madd.s and 19 lsi for about 16 products. So there is one fused multiply-add per product and the remainder is addressing, moves and loop control - between roughly 0.75 and 1.5 overhead instructions per product, which is where the ledger's 1.75 figure came from. It also explains why the wider variants lost when they were measured: kron2 four-across read -0.30% and the single-walk eight-across -0.18%, both because a wide row costs four registers and the shipped body deliberately re-reads 16 floats per j step - that re-reading is how it affords eight accumulators. With this the three largest phases are all accounted for from the image rather than from a summary: proj2bit (49.7%) at 24 forced ALU ops per 16 weights = 12 issue cycles + ~4 slack = the measured 16, with the only escape costing 4x the bytes; attention (14.6%) with FP contraction already ON, 119 madd.s against 58 mul.s and 29 add.s, so its fused budget is already spent; and hadamard (12.6%) at one madd per product with under 1.5 overhead instructions. Together with the earlier per-phase closures - engram at the LUT-GEMV floor, phi delivery-bound and unpaid, sinkhorn exp/log-bound, mix swept, transform measured on width, fusion, pass count and rescale placement - that is a complete account of where the 163 ms token goes and why none of it is addressable without changing what is stored, which the byte-exact and fidelity gates refuse. Caught and recorded a self-correction before publishing an over-reach, which is the same discipline this campaign applies to its gates applied to its own prose. I was about to record a tidy global claim - "every phase runs at the same effective IPC, therefore there is one bottleneck" - and the arithmetic refused it. Computing implied IPC from each phase's timer and its work: proj2bit 79.7 ms with 14.36 M weights at 2 instructions per weight gives 1.50 IPC; the engram's 14.6 ms with 2.36 M weights gives 1.35 IPC - both consistent with the walker's measured 1.33-1.5 and with the 24-ALU-ops-plus-slack accounting of #849. But phi came out at 0.16 IPC and hadamard at 0.38, which is absurd, and the fault is mine rather than the engine's: those phase timers bracket more than the multiply work (mhc_phi4 includes nd_cq_prepare and the LUT build alongside the GEMVs) and my hadamard product count was simply wrong. That is the ledger's own standing warning - "the timers overlap, do not sum them" - applied to a computation I nearly published as a finding. What IS supported, and now recorded: the two phases that are pure 2-bit walker work, proj2bit and the engram's GEMVs, run the same kernel at the same rate (1.50 and 1.35 IPC), so the walker's cost model generalises across the model where it applies; the other phases cannot be priced per weight from their timers at all, which is a statement about the instrumentation rather than about the code. The rule extracted for the backlog: never derive a per-operation rate from a phase timer whose bracket is not single-purpose, and when a phase looks anomalously slow per unit of work, suspect the attribution before the kernel - this is the second time this campaign has caught that class (#295's phi "4.3x gap" was a units error) and the first time it was caught before publication. No engine code changed, no board time spent, no metric moved; pins at B3 6.1450 / B2 6.1250 / B1 5.9283 with the best gated packet at 6.1433 = +15.8% over the accepted 5.3033.

Quantified the closure of the attention phase's hottest kernel using only measured numbers, which is what the #852 rule now requires - no rates derived from multi-purpose timers. The campaign's own kbench reports the shipping 48-dim QK dot at 139 cycles (KB DOT n=48 c4_pair_cyc=139), so 48 MACs in 139 cycles = 2.90 cycles per MAC against a roughly 1 MAC/cycle FPU: the kernel runs at 35% of peak and carries about 1.9 cycles of exposed latency per MAC that only the compiler's interleaving hides. That single measured number explains the entire measured history of this kernel and closes it with a reason rather than a shrug: pairing the two dots of a position pair cost -46% (404 cycles), four accumulators folded once cost -54% (214), a 128-bit assembly version cost -107% (286), and the wide-load DOT8W lost 2.1% and 1.9% in the field precisely because the hand-written body issued each madd immediately after its load, exposing the latency the C body hides. The win that did land in this phase - exp pairing, +19.96% in isolation - is a latency-hiding win, not an instruction-count win, which is the same lesson from the other direction. So the lever here is latency hiding and the compiler is the best scheduler measured for it; beating it would need a pipeline over the six 8-column chunks that four attempts failed to produce, and the one place a hand-written pipeline did win in this campaign was the two-deep codebook load in the wide phi, worth +0.028% - sub-bar. Recorded in the backlog with the table so no future window re-opens the QK dot without a concrete schedule that differs from all four. No engine code changed, no board time spent, no metric moved; pins at B3 6.1450 / B2 6.1250 / B1 5.9283 with the best gated packet at 6.1433 = +15.8% over the accepted 5.3033.

Built the quantified token model and recorded it in the handoff as an artifact a future window can check any proposal against - the last analysis this campaign's data supports, and a genuinely useful one. It reconciles every phase against MEASURED per-call costs rather than estimates, with the #852 rule in force (no rate derived from a multi-purpose timer): proj2bit's 79.7 ms is 14.36 M weights at 2 instructions each running at the walker's measured 1.50 IPC, and its 24 forced ALU ops per 16 weights explain the 16 cycles per word as 12 issue + ~4 slack; attention's 23.5 ms contains 14,400 QK dots at the measured 139 cycles each = 2.0 Mcycles = 8.3 ms, with the dot at 2.90 cycles per MAC (35% of FPU peak) and latency-bound; hadamard's 20.2 ms is kron_apply at the verified ~1 madd per product with under 1.5 overhead instructions; the engram's 14.6 ms is 2.36 M weights at the same 1.35 IPC as proj2bit, which is the same kernel; phi's 8.1 ms cannot be priced per weight because that timer's bracket includes prepare and the LUT build, which is a statement about the instrumentation; and the two phases with clean per-call costs both reconcile: sinkhorn's 3,786 exps at ~99 cycles plus 1,280 logf at ~350 gives 3.43 ms against a measured 3.0-3.7 ms, and prep+lut's 10-24 calls at a measured 37.4 kcycles each gives 1.56-3.75 ms against a measured 1.7-4.2 ms. Three properties make the table useful: every entry is a reconciliation rather than an estimate, the two pure walker phases agree on the same effective IPC so that cost model generalises, and nothing in it is addressable without changing what is stored - proj2bit by the ISA's addressing, attention by load latency the compiler already schedules best, hadamard by register pressure, the engram because it is the same kernel, sinkhorn because its transcendental calls are bit-exactness-locked, and phi because its residual is delivery needing ~18 KB/core that is not there. The handoff now tells a reader to find the phase a proposal targets, read the model column, and abandon the proposal if it does not change a count in it. No engine code changed, no board time spent, no metric moved; pins at B3 6.1450 / B2 6.1250 / B1 5.9283 with the best gated packet at 6.1433 = +15.8% over the accepted 5.3033.

Produced the first genuinely new candidate this campaign has had since the amortised loop, and it came out of the quantified model rather than out of guessing. The chain: the model says the QK dot costs a measured 139 cycles for 48 MACs = 2.90 cycles/MAC against a roughly 1 MAC/cycle FPU, i.e. about 1.9 cycles of exposed latency per MAC, and #853 established that four hand-written schedules and a wide-load variant all lost to the compiler's interleaving - which means none of them changed the thing that matters. What they had in common is that they attacked the BODY; none changed which operands are resident while the body runs. The observation: the traverse is position-outer and head-inner, so the two staged kf0/kf1 rows (384 bytes) are loaded once per position and then used for ONE head's 48 MACs, while the same two rows are re-loaded for each of the twelve heads sharing that kv position - twelve re-reads of an operand that changes once. The change: invert the block so the rows are staged once per kv position and all twelve heads' dots are computed against them, 576 MACs per 384 bytes instead of 48, with the twelve q rows (2.3 KB) resident in internal RAM. Bit-exact by construction: each head still sums its own 48 products in the same ascending order into the same accumulator, and its softmax/max/denom/rescale still runs in the same order afterwards; only the order in which different heads are visited changes, and heads are independent. Priced from measured numbers: if the blocked traverse lifts the dot from 2.90 to about 1.3 cycles/MAC, QK falls from 8.3 ms to ~3.7 ms = +2.8% of the token - and it is the same shape as the two blocking changes that did win here (wide phi, kron1), both of which paid because the compiler was re-reading an operand it could not keep. Risks recorded in order: register pressure forces the rows to be walked from internal RAM so the win depends on L1 rather than on values; the parallel split is already per-head so the blocking must apply within each core's range; and the staging helper's current shape assumes position-outer. Written into .auto/ideas.md and the queue for the next window to build, with no board time spent and no engine code changed; pins at B3 6.1450 / B2 6.1250 / B1 5.9283 with the best gated packet at 6.1433 = +15.8% over the accepted 5.3033.

Refuted my own candidate by checking its premise in the code before spending a board lane on it, and recorded the withdrawal. Last window I proposed a head-blocked QK traverse priced at +2.8%, on the argument that the two staged kf rows are re-loaded from memory for each of the twelve heads sharing a kv position. The code check says otherwise: kv_stage_pair (nd_model.c:73) is the noinline helper that converts four int8 values per 32-bit word out of the KV cache into fp32 STAGING buffers, and qk_dot8 takes const float *kf0, *kf1 - so the dot consumes already-staged fp32 rows from a small internal buffer, and the twelve re-reads are L1 hits a few kilobytes wide rather than memory traffic. Blocking the heads against that buffer would change loop structure without changing where the data comes from, so the load-traffic argument that justified the +2.8% does not hold. Where the dot's measured 2.90 cycles/MAC actually comes from is what #853 already established: the lsi-to-madd.s dependency inside the body, i.e. register/FPU load-use latency, which is precisely why four hand-written schedules and a wide-load variant all lost to the compiler's interleaving and why the one hand-written pipeline that did win here (two-deep codebook loads) was worth 0.028%. Disposition: withdrawn from the queue rather than built, with the withdrawal recorded in both the queue and the backlog along with what a future attempt would need to do first - measure the stall attribution inside the dot (a kbench variant isolating load-use stalls from issue) rather than arguing loop order again. This is the fourth time this session that checking a premise before pricing a lever has avoided a wasted lane, and the second time it caught my own reasoning. No board time spent, no engine code changed, no metric moved; pins at B3 6.1450 / B2 6.1250 / B1 5.9283 with the best gated packet at 6.1433 = +15.8% over the accepted 5.3033.

Corrected my own characterization of the QK dot and replaced the withdrawn candidate with a better-founded one. CORRECTION: #853 called the dot latency-bound because of its 2.90 cycles/MAC. Counting instructions refutes that - each of the 48 MACs needs lsi qhA[i] + lsi kf0[i] + madd.s = 3 instructions, so 48 MACs is 144 instructions in the measured 139 cycles = an implied IPC of 1.04, i.e. the kernel is ISSUE-bound at essentially full issue for what it executes, with no stall to attribute and no schedule to repair. That also explains the four failed schedules more sharply: they either added instructions or left the count unchanged. NEW CANDIDATE from the correction: the only lever on an issue-bound dot is fewer loads per MAC, and 64-bit float loads fetch two floats at once, taking a term pair to about 1.5-2 instructions per MAC instead of 3. The campaign did try wide-load QK bodies twice and lost 2.1%/1.9%, but the failure mode is known and specific: the hand-written bodies issued each madd immediately after the load it depended on, exposing load-use latency instead of hiding it. The missing ingredient is already shipped in this tree - the two-deep pipelining from the wide phi (#806), where each block's extui/addx4/lsi is issued before the previous block's madd.s with alternating registers, verified by objdump. Prize from measured numbers: 139 -> ~70 cycles per dot, so QK falls from 8.3 to ~4.2 ms = +2.5% of the token, larger than anything kept since the amortised loop. Build order recorded: write the pipelined 64-bit body; objdump-verify that loads are in flight ahead of their consumers (the exact check that caught #806's unreachable loop); host-gate before flashing because any re-association is a rounding change and the host oracle is where it must be caught; then the device goldens and the tree's own differential, screened against that tree's pin only. Written into the backlog and the queue as the next candidate, replacing the withdrawn one. No engine code changed, no board time spent, no metric moved; pins at B3 6.1450 / B2 6.1250 / B1 5.9283 with the best gated packet at 6.1433 = +15.8% over the accepted 5.3033.

Corrected my own basis twice before building anything, and the second correction is the one that matters for how the campaign prices things. FIRST: the kbench figure I used, KB DOT n=48 c4_pair_cyc=139, is a PAIR of dots - 96 MACs, not 48 - so the measured cost is 1.45 cycles/MAC, not the 2.90 I had been carrying since #853; my arithmetic had divided a pair figure by one dot's MAC count. SECOND, and more useful: counting the pair form's instructions shows it already shares the qh load across its two kf dots - 1 qh load + 2 kf loads + 2 madds per 2 MACs = 2.5 instructions per MAC - which at 1.45 cycles/MAC is an IPC of 1.73, i.e. 86% of the S3's 2-wide peak. So the dot is nearly ISSUE-SATURATED in that measurement, and a 64-bit-load body would take it to about 1.75 instructions/MAC against 2.5, i.e. 139 -> ~97 cycles, QK 8.3 -> ~5.8 ms = about +1.5% of the token rather than the +2.5% I first quoted. The candidate survives above the bar but at a smaller price. THE CAVEAT THAT DECIDES THE NEXT STEP: 139 cycles is a kbench figure - warm, isolated, back-to-back - and this campaign has paid three times (#295, #364, #745) to learn that a warm isolated number prices nothing, because the field dot runs inside a loop with staging and softmax around it. So the +1.5% is an estimate whose measurement structure does not match the field, and the honest next action is not to write the wide-load body but to re-price it with the field's call structure first - a small kbench variant that calls the dot once per group immediately followed by its consumer, exactly what the transform screen eventually had to do. Both corrections are recorded in the backlog with the arithmetic, so the next window starts from the right number and the right caveat. No engine code changed, no board time spent, no metric moved; pins at B3 6.1450 / B2 6.1250 / B1 5.9283 with the best gated packet at 6.1433 = +15.8% over the accepted 5.3033.

B1's record-bench crashed twice with the same fault, and the fault is diagnosed exactly - in the BENCH's context setup, not in the kernel and not in the clone. Evidence: LoadProhibited with EXCVADDR 0x0000001c, faulting code inside nd_lut2_rows_tie1n (the SHIPPING walker: base 0x4037b1dc, fault at 0x4037b244 = +0x68, LEND 0x4037b59e), and LCOUNT 0x00000005, which is six groups minus one - i.e. the fault happens INSIDE the group loop. Address 0x1c is 28 = seven times four, and the only index in that body that is a multiple of four below 64 is the pair-table lookup, whose base register is the LUT pointer from the context. So the walker is reading the pair table through a null base: my bench never got `lut` into the field the walker actually reads. I set `c.lut = lut` at six setup sites and the fault did not move, which means the kbench's view of the context struct does not match the engine's - a bench/ABI mismatch, exactly the class this campaign has been bitten by before when a bench carried its own copy of a shape. Consequence for the record: the layout experiment is NOT tested, NOT refuted - the differential has not run at all, because the crash is in the shipping walker's call from my bench. What IS established: the clone assembles in its own aligned section with the three-argument ABI and the three record edits; the bench builds records with `nd_f16(halfword)` as the stored norm so the clone's scale is exactly what NF16V would have produced; and the record arrays are real-sized (576 rows x 6 groups x 36 B = 124,416 B). Next step is one read of engine/include/nd_quant.h's actual context layout, then the bench sets the LUT field at the offset the walker uses (or calls the engine's own gemv entry with a proper context instead of hand-rolling one), and only then is the differential - and the timing - meaningful. Also this window: B3's dense Sinkhorn fixed-point exit is measured at 6.1467 vs 6.1450 (+0.028%, sub-bar, breadth running) with the host counter showing 1,217 iterations saved of 28,640; and B2's sparse variant (checks on passes 5/9/13/17) is built, host-green and running against its 6.1317 baseline. B1's record bench is still crashing, and this run taught me that my diagnosis chain was unsound - which is the honest content of this entry. Three facts in order. (1) Replacing my hand-rolled context with the ENGINE's own nd_lut2_fill, over a real tensor found by the kbench's existing find_tensor helper, changed nothing: identical LoadProhibited, identical EXCVADDR 0x0000001c, identical LBEG/LEND, identical LCOUNT 5. So the context construction was never the cause and the bench/ABI-mismatch theory is dead. (2) Last window's "0x1c = seven times four, so the pair-table base is null" reading is also dead, and for a reason worth recording: I added a print of the tensor metadata and the first context words immediately BEFORE the first walker call, and it never appeared on the wire despite an explicit fflush - so the crash happens earlier in bench_reco than the walker call my theory blamed. (3) The lesson that follows is about evidence: the panic's LBEG and LEND registers are simply the last values some hardware loop left in them, so pointing them at a function's address range is NOT identification of the faulting code - I had been treating them as such for two windows. The 36-byte record layout is MEASURED at last, on real bytes, and it loses: RECO rows=768 ng=6 packed_cyc=1577208 reco_cyc=1598440 pct=+1.35 mismatch=0 first=0. Two results in one line. CORRECTNESS: mismatch=0 over all 768 rows of a real CQ2 tensor, i.e. the record clone nd_lut2_rows_reco is bit-identical to the shipping walker on the archive's own packed bytes and fp16 norms, with the record norm stored as nd_f16(halfword) - exactly the value NF16V computes - and a non-zero activation so the LUT is non-trivial (an all-zero LUT would have made the comparison trivially exact). SPEED: the record layout costs 1.35% MORE cycles than the shipping packed-plus-separate-norms layout over the same rows. That is the expected sign once the line arithmetic is done properly: sixteen contiguous 36-byte records occupy 576 bytes, which is nine 64-byte lines - the same nine lines that 512 bytes of packed data plus the amortised norm bytes also occupy - so the layout saves no line traffic and pays +6.25% more bytes plus an unaligned 36-byte stride. The candidate is therefore closed as a measured loss, and closed on the mechanism rather than on the estimate: this is the first time the record idea was tested at all, and it took an engine boot self-test to do it, because the kbench image on this tree is unrunnable. THE METHOD THAT WORKED, worth recording because three attempts failed without it: one edit, then a build, then the next edit - the earlier failures were all placement and anchor errors inside a large hand-written C file, and the build catches each one for the price of a compile. The selftest itself must now be REMOVED before any device measurement: it runs inside nd_model_open, adds about 13 ms to boot, and is a diagnostic, not shipping code. State: B3 6.1467 (dense Sinkhorn exit, sub-bar, breadth complete), B2 running its sparse Sinkhorn lane against 6.1317, B1 back to its 5.9283 tree once the selftest and clone are lifted out.

Priced a fresh candidate and retired it unbuilt, which is the cheap half of this campaign's discipline working as intended. The idea: zcrms reduces one activation row with a SINGLE dependent accumulator (for (i...) ss += x[i]*x[i];), so with ~3 cycles of FP add latency the chain is latency-bound, and pairing two independent rows in one loop would hide that latency without reassociating either sum - bit-exact by construction, and the same FORM that just paid twice on the QK body (+0.081% composed) and the Sinkhorn detector (sparse better than dense by four times). The price came out sub-bar: 768 elements x 40 calls per token x 2 cycles saved per element = 0.26 ms of a 163 ms token = +0.157%, under the 0.2% bar even before the assumption is questioned - and the assumption is the weak part, since the 3-cycle latency is mine rather than measured and the symbol is inlined away in the ELF so confirming it needs a map-file lookup plus a caller-level disassembly for a prize that is already below the bar. Per the campaign's own rule - price before building, and if the price says sub-bar do not build - the idea is retired in the backlog with its arithmetic and with the condition that would reopen it (the zcrms family above ~1 ms/token, or a longer chain per call; the price scales linearly with elements x calls, so 768 x 200 would be +0.8% and worth a build). THE LESSON, now paid twice this session for the same mistake: a generator that rebuilds a hand-written assembly body by partitioning lines into blocks and 'the rest' must never assume where 'the rest' goes. The correct method, which is what the mentor prescribed for B3 and what worked there, is to splice the reordered block between two SPECIFIC neighbouring instructions (for this kernel: between the last ee.ldf and the loop-end label) and leave every other line exactly where it was. The objdump check - does the kernel's first instruction belong to the body's intended start - is the cheap guard that catches this in one command, and it did.
